GEN.about: The book of beginnings: of the world, of mankind, of sin, and of God’s plan to save. Its first eleven chapters tell of creation, the fall, the flood and Babel in the language of ancient story, teaching truths about God and man rather than giving a scientific account. From chapter 12 it follows Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, the fathers of Israel, to whom God binds himself by promise. The Church reads its promise of a victor over the serpent (3:15) as the first announcement of the Redeemer.
GEN.author: Tradition ascribes the first five books, the Pentateuch, to Moses. Most scholars today see them as the work of many hands over centuries, drawing on older traditions and taking final shape after the Exile. The Church leaves the question open while holding that Moses stands at the origin of Israel’s law and story.
GEN.date: Final form probably in the 6th or 5th century BC, from traditions much older.
GEN.setting: The stories of the patriarchs are set in the Near East of the second millennium BC, among the herdsmen and cities of Mesopotamia, Canaan and Egypt. The book as we have it spoke to an Israel that had lost its land and temple, reminding it that the God who made heaven and earth had chosen Abraham and would keep his word.
themes: Creation and the goodness of the world

key.note: God creates heaven and earth
The first promise of a Redeemer, the Protoevangelium
The call of Abraham: in him all nations blessed
The sacrifice of Isaac, a figure of Christ

sources: Pontifical Biblical Commission, The Interpretation of the Bible in the Church (1993)

EXO.about: The book of Israel’s liberation. God hears the cry of his people enslaved in Egypt, calls Moses at the burning bush and reveals his name (3:14). He brings Israel out through the plagues, the Passover and the crossing of the sea; at Sinai he gives the Ten Commandments and seals a covenant in blood (24:8); and even after the golden calf he forgives and comes to dwell among them in the tabernacle. The Church sees in the Passover lamb a figure of Christ, and in the crossing of the sea a figure of Baptism.
EXO.author: Tradition ascribes it, with the rest of the Pentateuch, to Moses, its central figure. Most scholars see it as woven from several older traditions and sources, some of them priestly, brought to final form after the Exile. The Church leaves the question open while honouring Moses as the mediator of the covenant and the law.
EXO.date: Final form probably in the 6th or 5th century BC, from much older traditions; many think the Song of the Sea (chapter 15) one of Israel’s oldest poems.
EXO.setting: The story opens with the descendants of Jacob enslaved in Egypt, building store cities for Pharaoh, one of them called Ramesses (1:11). Scholars who accept a historical core usually place it in the 13th century BC, under a pharaoh such as Ramesses II, though no Egyptian record mentions it and its date and scale are debated. Ever after, Israel remembered itself as a people of freed slaves, and later generations, the exiles in Babylon among them, hoped for a new exodus.
themes: God hears the cry of the oppressed

key.note: God reveals his name: I AM WHO AM
The Passover lamb and its saving blood, a figure of Christ
Israel crosses the sea on dry ground; Pharaoh’s army is drowned
The Ten Commandments given at Sinai

sources: Pontifical Biblical Commission, The Interpretation of the Bible in the Church (1993)

LEV.about: The handbook of Israel’s worship: laws for sacrifices, for the ordination of priests, for clean and unclean, and for the great Day of Atonement (chapter 16). At its centre stands God’s call, “Be ye holy, because I the Lord your God am holy” (19:2), which reaches into food, body, harvest, debts and dealings with neighbours. Jesus quotes its command to love one’s neighbour as oneself (19:18). The Letter to the Hebrews reads its sacrifices and high priest as figures fulfilled in Christ’s one sacrifice; Christians no longer keep its ritual laws, but its call to holiness remains.
LEV.author: Tradition ascribes it to Moses, who receives these laws at Sinai. Most scholars see it as the work of Israel’s priests, gathering the practice of the Jerusalem temple over generations; chapters 17–26, called the “Holiness Code”, may once have been a separate collection. The Church leaves the question of authorship open.
LEV.date: Final form probably in the 6th or 5th century BC; much of its ritual law is older, and some scholars date most of the book before the Exile.
LEV.setting: The book is set at the foot of Mount Sinai, in the month after the tabernacle was set up, as God speaks to Moses about worship. Its laws reflect long priestly practice in Israel’s sanctuaries and in the temple of Jerusalem. In its final form it spoke to a people who had lost their temple or were rebuilding it, teaching them that a holy God lived among them and that all of life, not only worship, belonged to him.
themes: Be holy, for God is holy

key.note: The Day of Atonement, which Hebrews sees fulfilled in Christ
Be ye holy, because I the Lord your God am holy
Seek no revenge; love thy friend as thyself, as Jesus taught
The jubilee: every fiftieth year, release and return to family land

sources: Pontifical Biblical Commission, The Jewish People and their Sacred Scriptures in the Christian Bible (2001)

NUM.about: The book of the journey through the wilderness, from Sinai to the plains of Moab on the edge of the promised land. It takes its name from two counts of the people (chapters 1 and 26). The first generation grumble, rebel and refuse to enter the land, and die in the desert; a new generation is counted in their place. Yet God goes on guiding, feeding and forgiving. Jesus speaks of the bronze serpent as a figure of his cross (John 3:14), and early Christian writers saw in Balaam’s star rising out of Jacob a sign of the Messiah.
NUM.author: Tradition ascribes it, with the rest of the Pentateuch, to Moses. Most scholars see it as combining priestly lists and laws with older stories and poems, among them the oracles of Balaam, brought to final form after the Exile. The Church leaves the question of authorship open.
NUM.date: Final form probably in the 6th or 5th century BC, from older traditions; the poetic oracles of Balaam may be among the oldest parts.
NUM.setting: The book spans some forty years in the deserts south of Canaan and the lands east of the Jordan, ending across the river from Jericho. Israel camps by tribes around the tabernacle and moves when the cloud moves. Edom, Moab and Midian appear as neighbours and rivals. An inscription of about 800 BC, found at Deir Alla in Jordan, tells of a seer named Balaam son of Beor, so his name lived on in the region’s own traditions.
themes: A new generation inherits the promise

key.note: The priestly blessing: The Lord bless thee, and keep thee
God forgives, yet the unbelieving generation will not see the land
The bronze serpent: whoever is bitten and looks on it lives
Balaam’s oracle: a star shall rise out of Jacob

DEU.about: Moses’ farewell: a series of speeches on the plains of Moab, retelling the journey from Sinai and setting out the law again for the generation about to enter the land (its name means “second law”). Its heart is the Shema, “Hear, O Israel” (6:4–5): there is one Lord, to be loved with the whole heart, soul and strength. It calls Israel to remember, to obey and to choose life. Jesus answered the tempter in its words and called its command of love the greatest; the Church sees in the prophet like Moses whom it promises (18:15) a figure of Christ.
DEU.author: Tradition ascribes it to Moses, apart from the account of his death, which one Jewish tradition credits to Joshua. Most scholars link its core with the “book of the law” found in the Temple under King Josiah (2 Kings 22), shaped by circles of priests and scribes and expanded during the Exile. The Church leaves the question open.
DEU.date: Its core probably took shape in the 7th century BC, around King Josiah’s reform of 622 BC, with additions during the Exile in the 6th century.
DEU.setting: Moses speaks on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho, at the end of the forty years. Scholars connect the book with Judah in the 7th century BC, when King Josiah, after years of Assyrian domination, used a book of the law found in the Temple to purge idolatry and centre worship in Jerusalem. Its form recalls ancient treaties between great kings and their vassals. To the exiles in Babylon it explained the loss of the land and still set before them the choice of life.
themes: Love God with all your heart
One God, one people, one sanctuary
Care for the poor, widow and stranger

key.note: The Shema: Hear, O Israel; love the Lord with thy whole heart
Manna in the desert: not in bread alone doth man live
God will raise up a prophet like Moses
Life and death set before Israel: choose life

sources: Moshe Weinfeld, Deuteronomy and the Deuteronomic School

JOS.about: Israel, led by Moses’ successor, crosses the Jordan, takes the land of Canaan and divides it among the tribes; before he dies, Joshua binds the people to serve the Lord alone (chapter 24). The book celebrates God’s faithfulness: not one of his promises failed (21:43). Its accounts of war, and of whole cities destroyed under the “ban”, are hard reading; the Church asks that such passages be read in their historical setting and in the light of Christ. Joshua’s name, “the Lord saves”, is the same as Jesus’, and the Fathers saw him as a figure of Christ leading his people into their rest.
JOS.author: Jewish tradition (the Talmud) ascribes the book to Joshua himself, with the account of his death added by others. Many scholars see it as the first part of a great history running from Joshua to 2 Kings, written in the spirit of Deuteronomy in the late monarchy and the Exile, from older stories, lists and boundary records.
JOS.date: Probably compiled in the 7th and 6th centuries BC, from older traditions; the events it tells are set around 1200 BC.
JOS.setting: The story is set around 1200 BC, at the end of the Late Bronze Age, when Canaan was a patchwork of small city states under fading Egyptian control. Archaeology shows many new villages appearing in the hill country then, widely thought to be early Israel, but most archaeologists find no sign of a single swift conquest; Jericho, for instance, seems to have had no walled city at the time. Judges 1 itself describes a slower, partial settlement.
themes: Choosing to serve the Lord alone
The faith of an outsider, Rahab

key.note: Take courage, and be strong: the Lord is with thee
The ark goes first, and Israel crosses the Jordan on dry ground
At the trumpets and the shout, the walls of Jericho fall
Choose this day whom you will serve; Joshua’s house will serve the Lord

JOS.canon: Called Josue in the Douay-Rheims. In the Hebrew Bible it is the first of the “Former Prophets”, the books from Joshua to Kings.
sources: Amihai Mazar, Archaeology of the Land of the Bible

JDG.about: Israel in the land before it had kings, told through a repeating cycle: the people forsake the Lord, fall to their enemies and cry out, and God raises up a “judge”, a deliverer, to save them (2:11–19). Among them are Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah and Samson, flawed and surprising heroes. The book grows darker as it goes, ending in idolatry, atrocity and civil war, when “every one did that which seemed right to himself” (21:24). It shows the patience of God and the need for a faithful king; the Letter to the Hebrews counts Gideon, Samson and Jephthah among the heroes of faith.
JDG.author: Jewish tradition (the Talmud) ascribes it to Samuel. Most scholars see it as part of the great history running from Joshua to 2 Kings, written in the spirit of Deuteronomy, which set old hero stories of the tribes within a framework of sin, punishment and deliverance.
JDG.date: Probably compiled in the 7th or 6th century BC; the Song of Deborah (chapter 5) is thought to be one of the oldest Hebrew poems, perhaps from the 12th or 11th century BC.
JDG.setting: The book is set between Joshua’s death and the first king, roughly 1200–1050 BC. Israel was then a loose league of tribes in the hill country, with no capital and no standing army, pressed by Canaanite kings, by Moab and Ammon, by Midianite raiders, and by the Philistines, newly settled on the coast. An Egyptian victory inscription of about 1208 BC already names Israel as a people in Canaan. For later readers the book showed how unfaithfulness leads to ruin.
themes: The longing for a faithful king

key.note: The pattern of the book: sin, oppression, a judge, relapse
Gideon called: The Lord is with thee, O most valiant of men
An angel announces Samson’s birth to a barren woman
No king in Israel: every one did what seemed right to himself

sources: Amihai Mazar, Archaeology of the Land of the Bible

RUT.about: A short story of loyalty and kindness. Naomi, widowed and bereaved in Moab, returns to Bethlehem with her Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth, who will not leave her: “Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God” (1:16). Gleaning in the fields of Boaz, a kinsman, Ruth finds favour; he redeems the family’s land and marries her, and their son Obed becomes David’s grandfather. Ruth appears in Matthew’s genealogy of Jesus. Christians have seen in this foreign woman welcomed into Israel a sign that all nations are called, and in Boaz the redeemer a figure of Christ.
RUT.author: Jewish tradition (the Talmud) ascribes it to Samuel. The author is in fact unknown, a storyteller of great skill and tenderness.
RUT.date: Uncertain. Some scholars place it under the monarchy, perhaps in the 10th to 8th century BC; many date it after the Exile, in the 5th or 4th century BC.
RUT.setting: The story is set “when the judges ruled” (1:1), in Bethlehem and in Moab, east of the Dead Sea, a farming world of famine and harvest. It turns on Israel’s laws for the poor and for the family: the right to glean (Leviticus 19:9–10), the redeeming of land (Leviticus 25:25), and the raising up of a dead man’s name (compare Deuteronomy 25:5–10). If written after the Exile, it may gently answer those who would shut out foreigners, since David himself had a Moabite great-grandmother.
themes: The outsider welcomed into God’s people

key.note: Ruth to Naomi: thy people shall be my people, thy God my God
Boaz blesses the foreigner who has fled under God’s wings
Ruth asks Boaz, a near kinsman, to spread his covering over her
Obed is born: the father of Jesse, the father of David

RUT.canon: Greek and Latin Bibles, and so the Douay-Rheims, place Ruth after Judges. In the Hebrew Bible it stands among the Writings and is read at the feast of Weeks (Pentecost).

1SA.about: The story of Israel’s passage from judges to kings. It opens with Hannah, a barren woman whose prayer is answered with Samuel, the last judge and a great prophet. When the people demand a king like the nations, God gives them Saul, who fails through disobedience, and then chooses David, a shepherd boy, on whom the Spirit of the Lord comes. The book follows David’s rise, his friendship with Jonathan and his flight from Saul, until Saul dies in battle. Hannah’s song (2:1–10) is echoed in Mary’s Magnificat, and the Lord’s anointed king points to Christ, the Anointed One.
1SA.author: Jewish tradition (the Talmud) says Samuel wrote the book up to his death and the prophets Gad and Nathan completed it. Most scholars see 1 and 2 Samuel as part of the great history running from Joshua to 2 Kings, built from older sources such as a story of the ark and a story of David’s rise.
1SA.date: Probably compiled in the 7th or 6th century BC, from sources some of which may be much older, perhaps from not long after David’s time (about 1000 BC).
1SA.language: Hebrew; the Greek and the Dead Sea Scrolls help restore its text
1SA.setting: Around 1050–1000 BC the tribes of Israel were hard pressed by the Philistines, a people of Aegean origin settled on the southern coast, who even captured the ark of the covenant. With no standing army or central government, Israel looked for a king. The book follows the change from a league of tribes to a monarchy, and asks what a king of God’s people should be: not one who trusts in his own strength, but one who listens to God.
themes: Kingship: the people’s demand and God’s choice

key.note: Hannah’s song, echoed centuries later in Mary’s Magnificat
The boy Samuel: Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth
David anointed: man sees appearances, but the Lord beholds the heart
David faces Goliath in the name of the Lord of hosts

1SA.canon: Called 1 Kings in the Douay-Rheims, which follows the Latin Vulgate in calling 1 and 2 Samuel and 1 and 2 Kings the four books of Kings. In Hebrew, Samuel was a single book; the Greek translation first divided it.
sources: P. Kyle McCarter, I Samuel (Anchor Bible)

2SA.about: The story of David’s reign. He becomes king over Judah and then over all Israel, takes Jerusalem and brings the ark there with dancing and joy. Through the prophet Nathan, God promises him a house, a line of kings whose throne will stand for ever (chapter 7): the root of Israel’s hope for the Messiah, the Son of David. But David sins gravely with Bathsheba and against her husband Uriah, repents when Nathan confronts him, and lives through the bitter revolt of his son Absalom. The angel’s promise to Mary echoes Nathan’s words (Luke 1:32–33).
2SA.author: Jewish tradition (the Talmud) holds that Samuel’s book was completed by the prophets Gad and Nathan, who knew David. Most scholars see it as part of the great history running from Joshua to 2 Kings. Chapters 9–20, on the struggle for David’s throne, are often admired as a masterpiece of early history writing; some date them close to David’s court, others much later.
2SA.date: Probably compiled in the 7th or 6th century BC, from older sources; David reigned about 1010–970 BC.
2SA.language: Hebrew; the Greek and the Dead Sea Scrolls help restore its text
2SA.setting: The book covers David’s reign, about 1010–970 BC. He united the southern tribe of Judah with the northern tribes, took the old Canaanite city of Jerusalem from the Jebusites, made it his capital and brought the ark there, joining throne and worship in one place. Archaeologists debate how large and wealthy his kingdom was, but an Aramaic inscription of the 9th century BC, found at Tel Dan, names the “House of David”.
themes: Jerusalem, city of God and of the king
The cost of sin in a family

key.note: David dances with all his might as the ark is brought up
Nathan’s oracle: the throne of David’s son established for ever
Thou art the man: David confesses, and the Lord takes away his sin
David weeps for his rebel son: Absalom my son

2SA.canon: Called 2 Kings in the Douay-Rheims, which follows the Latin Vulgate in calling 1 and 2 Samuel and 1 and 2 Kings the four books of Kings. In Hebrew, Samuel was a single book; the Greek translation first divided it.
sources: P. Kyle McCarter, II Samuel (Anchor Bible)
Avraham Biran and Joseph Naveh, “An Aramaic Stele Fragment from Tel Dan”, Israel Exploration Journal 43 (1993)

1KI.about: The book opens with the death of David and the reign of Solomon, famed for the wisdom he asked of God and for building the Temple in Jerusalem, which the glory of the Lord filled. But Solomon’s heart turned to other gods, and after him the kingdom split in two: Israel in the north and Judah in the south. The rest of the book follows their kings, judged by their faithfulness to the Lord, and the prophet Elijah’s lonely struggle against the worship of Baal under King Ahab. Jesus spoke of “a greater than Solomon”, and Elijah appeared with him at the Transfiguration.
1KI.author: Jewish tradition (the Talmud) ascribes 1 and 2 Kings, originally one book, to the prophet Jeremiah. Most scholars see them as the last part of a great history running from Joshua onward, written in the spirit of Deuteronomy. The author names his sources, royal annals now lost, such as “the book of the words of the days of the kings of Juda”.
1KI.date: Probably first compiled under King Josiah, late in the 7th century BC, and completed during the Exile, after the last event in 2 Kings (about 561 BC).
1KI.setting: The book runs from about 970 to 850 BC. Solomon’s kingdom split after his death, about 930 BC: the larger northern kingdom of Israel, later ruled from Samaria, and the southern kingdom of Judah, with Jerusalem and the Temple. Both lived among greater powers, Egypt, Aram and a rising Assyria; an Assyrian inscription records King Ahab at a battle in 853 BC. Writing for a people that had lost its land, the author asks why.

key.note: Solomon asks God for an understanding heart
Heaven cannot contain God, yet he hears prayer in his house
Elijah on Carmel: fire falls, and the people cry, The Lord is God
Elijah, fed by an angel, meets God at Horeb in a gentle air

1KI.canon: Called 3 Kings in the Douay-Rheims, which follows the Latin Vulgate in calling 1 and 2 Samuel and 1 and 2 Kings the four books of Kings. In Hebrew, 1 and 2 Kings were a single book.

2KI.about: The story of the two kingdoms carried to its bitter end. It opens with Elijah taken up to heaven and the wonders of Elisha, who heals the Syrian general Naaman and feeds a hundred men with twenty loaves. Then the northern kingdom falls to Assyria (chapter 17), and Judah, despite the reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah, falls to Babylon: Jerusalem and the Temple are burned and the people led into exile. Yet the book closes with David’s heir released from prison, a thread of hope. Jesus recalled Naaman’s healing, and the Fathers saw in his washing in the Jordan a figure of Baptism.
2KI.author: Jewish tradition (the Talmud) ascribes 1 and 2 Kings, originally one book, to the prophet Jeremiah. Most scholars see them as the last part of a great history running from Joshua onward, written in the spirit of Deuteronomy, probably first under Josiah and then revised in exile. The author draws on royal annals now lost and on stories of the prophets.
2KI.date: Probably first compiled under King Josiah, late in the 7th century BC, and completed in exile after about 561 BC, where its story ends.
2KI.setting: The book runs from about 850 BC to the Exile. Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BC and scattered its people. Judah survived Sennacherib’s siege of Jerusalem in 701 BC, which the Assyrian king’s own annals record, but fell to Babylon: the city and its Temple were destroyed in 587 or 586 BC and many were deported. For the exiles the book gave an honest account of why it happened, and a call to return to God.
themes: The power of the prophetic word
Reform and return to the covenant

key.note: Elijah taken up in a whirlwind; Elisha takes up his mantle
Naaman washes in the Jordan and is made clean
The book of the law found in the Temple under Josiah
Jerusalem and the Temple burned; the people carried away to Babylon

2KI.canon: Called 4 Kings in the Douay-Rheims, which follows the Latin Vulgate in calling 1 and 2 Samuel and 1 and 2 Kings the four books of Kings. In Hebrew, 1 and 2 Kings were a single book.
sources: Mordechai Cogan and Hayim Tadmor, II Kings (Anchor Bible)

1CH.about: Israel’s story retold from a new angle. Nine chapters of family lists run from Adam to those who lived in Jerusalem after the exile, binding them to the whole history of God’s people. The rest is given to David, presented above all as the founder of Israel’s worship: he brings the ark to Jerusalem, orders the priests, Levites and singers, and prepares everything for the Temple his son Solomon will build. God’s promise of an everlasting kingdom to David’s son (chapter 17) kept alive the hope for the Messiah. Saint Jerome thought no one could claim to know the Scriptures without these books.
1CH.author: Jewish tradition (the Talmud) connects Chronicles with Ezra the scribe. Most scholars speak instead of an unknown “Chronicler”, perhaps a Levite of Jerusalem, who used Samuel and Kings and other sources. Whether he also wrote Ezra and Nehemiah, which continue the story, is debated; many now think not.
1CH.date: Probably in the 4th century BC, under Persian rule; its family lists run several generations past the return from exile in 538 BC.
1CH.setting: Written for the small community of Judah, then a province of the Persian empire, gathered round the rebuilt Temple in Jerusalem but with no king. Retelling the story from Adam to the Exile, the Chronicler shows them that they are the heirs of all Israel, that God’s promises to David still stand, and that faithful worship, with its priests, Levites and singers, is the heart of their life.
themes: David and the promise of an everlasting kingdom
Seeking God with a whole heart

key.note: A psalm of praise when the ark is brought to Jerusalem
Nathan’s oracle: David’s son set in God’s house and kingdom for ever
David to Solomon: serve God with a perfect heart; seek and find
David’s prayer: thine, O Lord, is the kingdom

1CH.canon: Called 1 Paralipomenon in the Douay-Rheims, from the Greek title meaning “things left out”, as if a supplement to Samuel and Kings; Saint Jerome suggested the name “Chronicle”. In Hebrew, 1 and 2 Chronicles are a single book.
sources: Jerome, Preface to the Books of Kings (Prologus Galeatus)
Sara Japhet, I and II Chronicles (Old Testament Library)
H. G. M. Williamson, Israel in the Books of Chronicles

2CH.about: The story continues from Solomon’s Temple to the Exile, following only the kings of Judah, David’s line. Solomon builds and dedicates the Temple; fire comes down from heaven and the Lord’s glory fills the house. Each later king is measured by how he seeks the Lord and cares for his house: reforming kings such as Hezekiah and Josiah are honoured, and even wicked Manasseh repents and is restored. When people and priests mock God’s messengers, Jerusalem falls; yet the book ends with Cyrus of Persia inviting the exiles to go up and rebuild. Its message is that God hears those who humble themselves and seek him.
2CH.author: Jewish tradition (the Talmud) connects Chronicles with Ezra the scribe. Most scholars speak instead of an unknown “Chronicler”, perhaps a Levite of Jerusalem, who used Samuel and Kings and other sources. Whether he also wrote Ezra and Nehemiah, which continue the story, is debated; many now think not.
2CH.date: Probably in the 4th century BC, under Persian rule, well over a century after the return from exile in 538 BC.
2CH.setting: Written for Judah under Persian rule, a small people round the rebuilt Temple, with no king of David’s line on the throne. The Chronicler retells the history of Judah from Solomon (about 970 BC) to the fall of Jerusalem (587 or 586 BC) and the decree of Cyrus (538 BC), to show that faithfulness is blessed and that repentance always finds God’s mercy. The northern kingdom appears only where it touches Judah.
themes: The Temple at the heart of Israel’s life
Seek the Lord and he will hear

key.note: Fire from heaven and the Lord’s glory fill Solomon’s Temple
If my people seek my face and repent, I will forgive and heal
Manasseh, taken captive, repents, and God hears his prayer
Cyrus’s decree to rebuild the Temple: let him go up

2CH.canon: Called 2 Paralipomenon in the Douay-Rheims, from the Greek title meaning “things left out”. In most printed Hebrew Bibles, Chronicles comes last, so that the Hebrew Scriptures end with Cyrus’s call to go up to Jerusalem.
sources: Jerome, Preface to the Books of Kings (Prologus Galeatus)
Sara Japhet, I and II Chronicles (Old Testament Library)
H. G. M. Williamson, 1 and 2 Chronicles (New Century Bible)

EZR.about: The story of a people starting again. When the Persian king Cyrus lets the exiles go home, a first group returns to Jerusalem and, after long delays, rebuilds the temple, finished in 515 BC (chapters 1–6). Later Ezra, priest and scribe, comes from Babylon with the law of Moses and calls the community to faithfulness, even to the painful step of sending away foreign wives (chapters 7–10). The book shows God keeping his word through the prophets, moving even pagan kings, and gathering a remnant around his house and his law. Saint Bede read the rebuilding as a figure of Christ building up his Church.
EZR.author: Jewish tradition (the Talmud) names Ezra as the writer. Most scholars today see Ezra and Nehemiah as one work put together by a later editor, who used Ezra’s own first-person memoir, lists of returning families and official letters. Whether the same hand also wrote Chronicles, as was long thought, is now debated.
EZR.date: Probably put together between about 400 and 300 BC, from memoirs, lists and letters of the century and a half before.
EZR.language: Hebrew, with official letters and records in Aramaic (4:8–6:18; 7:12–26)
EZR.setting: In 539 BC Cyrus of Persia took Babylon and allowed exiled peoples to return home. The Jews who came back found Jerusalem in ruins, their neighbours hostile and themselves few and poor. Judah was now a small province of the Persian Empire, with no king; the temple, the priesthood and the law of Moses held the people together. Whether Ezra arrived in 458 BC, before Nehemiah, or in 398 BC, after him, is still debated.
themes: Return from exile and a new beginning
God at work through pagan kings
The law of Moses taught and lived
Repentance and the purity of the community

key.note: Cyrus’s decree: the exiles may go home and rebuild the temple
The temple’s foundation laid amid shouts of joy and weeping
Ezra sets his heart to seek, do and teach the law
Ezra’s prayer of confession for the sins of his people

EZR.canon: Called 1 Esdras in the Douay-Rheims (not the different book called 1 Esdras in some other Bibles). Ezra and Nehemiah were counted as one book in the Hebrew Bible; Christian Bibles divide it in two.

NEH.about: Nehemiah, a Jew serving at the Persian court, hears that Jerusalem lies broken and disgraced, and wins the king’s leave to rebuild its walls. Told largely in his own words, the book shows a man of prayer and action: he organises the work, faces down mockers and enemies, and defends the poor against those who exploit them. At its heart (chapters 8–10) Ezra reads the law to the assembled people, who weep, rejoice and renew the covenant. It teaches that God’s work needs both prayer and courage, and that a people is rebuilt around his word.
NEH.author: The book opens as “the words of Nehemiah”, and tradition took him, or Ezra, as its writer. Its core is Nehemiah’s own memoir, written in the first person and marked by the prayer “Remember me, O my God”. Most scholars think a later editor joined this memoir to the Ezra material and added lists of names and the account of the covenant renewal.
NEH.date: Nehemiah’s memoir probably dates from about 430 BC; the book reached its final form with Ezra, probably between 400 and 300 BC.
NEH.setting: Nehemiah was cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes I. In 445 BC he came to Jerusalem as governor of Judah, a small province ringed by rivals such as Sanballat of Samaria and Tobiah the Ammonite. Nearly a century after the first return, the city was thinly peopled and its walls still in ruins. He governed for twelve years, went back to the king, and then returned to correct abuses that had crept in.
themes: The word of God read and understood

key.note: Nehemiah fasts and prays on hearing of Jerusalem’s ruin
The builders work with one hand and hold a sword with the other
The wall finished in fifty-two days: the enemies see God’s work
Ezra reads the law: “the joy of the Lord is our strength”

NEH.canon: Called 2 Esdras in the Douay-Rheims. In the Hebrew Bible it forms one book with Ezra.

TOB.about: A warm family story of faith in exile. Tobit, a devout Israelite in Nineveh, is blinded after doing works of mercy; far away, his kinswoman Sarah is tormented by a demon. God hears both their prayers and sends the angel Raphael, disguised as a travelling companion, with Tobit’s son Tobias. The journey brings healing, a holy marriage and a hymn of praise. The book teaches prayer, fasting and almsgiving, care for the dead and reverence for marriage. It is the Church’s source for the archangel Raphael, and its wedding-night prayer is among the readings for weddings.
TOB.author: The book presents itself as Tobit’s own story, and older tradition took it as such. Most scholars today, Catholic ones among them, read it as an edifying story written to teach by an unknown devout Jew, perhaps living outside the land of Israel, rather than as a strict historical record. The Church has not defined its literary form.
TOB.date: Probably about 225–175 BC, since it shows no sign of the persecution under Antiochus IV (167 BC).
TOB.language: Probably Aramaic; complete in Greek, with Aramaic and Hebrew fragments from Qumran
TOB.setting: The story is set in the 8th and 7th centuries BC among Israelites of the northern tribes, deported to Assyria when their kingdom fell, with scenes in Nineveh and Media. It was written centuries later for Jews scattered among the nations, who had to keep faith, the law and their family ties without temple or homeland, among neighbours who did not know God.
themes: Burying the dead as a work of mercy

key.note: Both prayers are heard, and Raphael is sent to heal them
Never do to another what you would hate done to you
Tobias and Sarah pray together on their wedding night
Raphael reveals himself, one of the seven who stand before the Lord

TOB.canon: Called Tobias in the Douay-Rheims, where father and son share that name. One of the deuterocanonical books, those not in the Jewish Bible: Catholics and the Orthodox receive it as Scripture (Councils of Hippo and Carthage, 393–397; Florence, 1442; Trent, 1546); Protestants generally do not.
sources: Council of Trent, Decree on the Canonical Scriptures (1546)
Joseph A. Fitzmyer, Tobit (Commentaries on Early Jewish Literature)

JDT.about: When the vast army of Holofernes besieges the little Israelite town of Bethulia, its leaders lose heart and give God five days to save them. Judith, a devout widow, rebukes them for putting God to the test, prays, and goes with only her maid into the enemy camp, where she beheads Holofernes and delivers her people. It is a story of God saving through the weak and humble, through prayer, fasting and courage. The Church has long seen in Judith a figure of Mary, and applies to Mary the people’s praise of Judith: “Thou art the glory of Jerusalem.”
JDT.author: Unknown. The book names no author, and tradition settled on none. Most scholars, Catholic and other, read it as a story written to teach rather than a chronicle: it makes Nebuchadnezzar king of the Assyrians at Nineveh and blends names and events from different centuries, perhaps deliberately, so that he stands for every enemy of God’s people. The Church has not defined its literary form.
JDT.date: Probably in the later 2nd century BC, after the Maccabean revolt, though some scholars place it a little earlier.
JDT.language: Probably Hebrew, now lost; Greek survives, and Jerome used an Aramaic text
JDT.setting: The story is placed in a deliberately mixed world: an Assyrian Nebuchadnezzar ruling from Nineveh, generals with Persian names, and Jews newly returned from exile. Its real background is probably the age of the Maccabees, when the Jews of Judea had resisted a pagan king who tried to force his gods on them, and had won. It encouraged a small people facing great powers to trust God, keep his law and never despair.
themes: Do not put God to the test
Judith as a figure of Mary

key.note: Judith rebukes the elders for testing God and setting him a deadline
Judith’s prayer: God’s power is not in numbers; he hears the humble
Ozias blesses Judith “above all women upon the earth”
“Thou art the glory of Jerusalem”, sung of Mary in the liturgy

JDT.canon: One of the deuterocanonical books, those not in the Jewish Bible: Catholics and the Orthodox receive it as Scripture (Councils of Hippo and Carthage, 393–397; Florence, 1442; Trent, 1546); Protestants generally do not. Jerome’s Latin, followed here, is shorter than the Greek and numbered differently.
sources: Council of Trent, Decree on the Canonical Scriptures (1546)

EST.about: Esther, a Jewish orphan raised by her kinsman Mordecai, becomes queen of Persia. When the king’s minister Haman plots to destroy the Jews, she risks her life by going to the king unbidden, and her people are saved; the feast of Purim remembers it. In the Hebrew book God is never named, yet his hidden hand is everywhere. The Greek additions, which the Church receives, make the prayer and faith explicit. Tradition sees in Esther, the queen who intercedes with the king for her people, a figure of Mary.
EST.author: Unknown. Jewish tradition (the Talmud) credited the men of the Great Assembly; some have named Mordecai, since the book says he wrote these things down (9:20). Most scholars think an unknown Jew of the eastern Diaspora wrote the Hebrew book, and that the Greek additions came later from other hands.
EST.date: The Hebrew book probably in the 4th or 3rd century BC. By its closing note (11:1), the Greek version reached Egypt in the late 2nd or early 1st century BC.
EST.language: Hebrew; the additions in Greek, some perhaps translated from Hebrew or Aramaic
EST.setting: The story is set in Susa, at the court of the Persian king Ahasuerus (called Artaxerxes in the Greek additions), usually identified with Xerxes I (486–465 BC). It speaks to Jews scattered through a foreign empire, loyal subjects yet always exposed to an enemy’s hatred, and assures them that God has not forgotten them. Some details do not fit what is known of Persian history, and many scholars read it as a story told to explain and hallow the feast of Purim.
themes: The proud brought low, the lowly raised

key.note: Mordecai: perhaps you came to the kingdom for such a time as this
Esther pleads for her people and names Haman as their enemy
Mordecai establishes the yearly feast of Purim
Esther’s prayer (Greek addition): help me, who have no helper but you

EST.canon: All Christians receive the Hebrew book. The Greek version adds six passages (among them a dream, prayers and royal letters) which Catholics and the Orthodox receive as Scripture, as Trent affirmed; Protestants generally do not. Jerome moved them to the end, so in the Douay-Rheims they stand at 10:4–16:24.
sources: Council of Trent, Decree on the Canonical Scriptures (1546)
Carey A. Moore, Daniel, Esther and Jeremiah: The Additions (Anchor Bible)

1MA.about: The story of the Jewish resistance to Antiochus IV, the Greek king who tried to stamp out the faith of Israel, and of the family who led it: the priest Mattathias and his sons Judas Maccabeus, Jonathan and Simon. It tells of martyrs, of guerrilla war, of the purifying of the defiled temple and the founding of the feast of Dedication, at which Jesus was later present in the temple (John 10:22–23), and of Judea’s hard-won freedom. Sober and close to the events, it shows faithfulness to God’s law valued above life itself.
1MA.author: Unknown: a devout Jew of Judea, probably writing in Jerusalem, well informed, who admired the Maccabean family and quotes official letters and documents. Tradition gave him no name. The title comes from Judas’s nickname, Maccabeus, usually explained as “the hammer”.
1MA.date: Probably about 100 BC: its closing verses (16:23–24) look back on the rule of John Hyrcanus (134–104 BC).
1MA.language: Hebrew, now lost; survives in Greek
1MA.setting: After Alexander the Great, Judea was ruled by Greek kings, first from Egypt, then from about 200 BC from Syria (the Seleucids). Greek ways attracted many Jews. In 167 BC Antiochus IV banned the law, the sabbath and circumcision and set up a pagan altar in the temple. The book covers 175–134 BC, from his accession to the death of Simon, the last of the brothers.
themes: Faithfulness to God’s law unto death

key.note: The “abominable idol of desolation” set on the altar; books of the law burnt
Mattathias refuses the king’s order to forsake the law
“Every one that hath zeal for the law… let him follow me”
The altar rededicated and the eight-day feast of Dedication established

1MA.canon: Called 1 Machabees in the Douay-Rheims. One of the deuterocanonical books, those not in the Jewish Bible: Catholics and the Orthodox receive it as Scripture (Councils of Hippo and Carthage, 393–397; Florence, 1442; Trent, 1546); Protestants generally do not, though they value it as history.
sources: Jerome, Preface to the Books of Kings (Prologus Galeatus)
Council of Trent, Decree on the Canonical Scriptures (1546)
Jonathan A. Goldstein, I Maccabees (Anchor Bible)

2MA.about: Not a sequel but a second account of the same struggle, from shortly before Antiochus IV’s reign to Judas Maccabeus’s victory over Nicanor in 161 BC. Written to move and teach as well as inform, it dwells on the martyrdom of the aged Eleazar and of a mother and her seven sons, on God’s care for his temple and on his mercy. It is a key Old Testament witness to the resurrection of the body, to creation out of nothing and to prayer for the dead, and the Catechism draws on it for each.
2MA.author: The writer, whose name is unknown, says he has abridged into one book a five-volume history by Jason of Cyrene, now lost (2:24). He was a Jew of Greek education. Two letters from Jerusalem to the Jews of Egypt, urging them to keep the feast of the temple’s purification, stand at the head of the book (1:1–2:19).
2MA.date: Jason’s history probably soon after 161 BC; the abridgement probably in the late 2nd century BC, though some date it later. A letter at its head is dated 124 BC (1:10).
2MA.setting: Under the Seleucid kings of Syria the high priesthood was bought and sold, and Jerusalem was split between those who embraced Greek ways and those who held fast to the law. Then came the persecution of Antiochus IV and the Maccabean revolt. The book is addressed to the large Jewish community of Egypt, to bind it to Jerusalem and its temple and to strengthen it in faith under trial.
themes: God’s care for his temple and people

key.note: The aged scribe Eleazar chooses death rather than break the law
A martyr: the King of the world will raise us up
The mother: God made heaven and earth out of nothing
Sacrifice offered for the dead: “a holy and wholesome thought”

2MA.canon: Called 2 Machabees in the Douay-Rheims. One of the deuterocanonical books, those not in the Jewish Bible: Catholics and the Orthodox receive it as Scripture (Councils of Hippo and Carthage, 393–397; Florence, 1442; Trent, 1546); Protestants generally do not.
sources: Jerome, Preface to the Books of Kings (Prologus Galeatus)
Council of Trent, Decree on the Canonical Scriptures (1546)

JOB.about: Job, a just man, loses his children, his wealth and his health, and sits scraping his sores. Three friends insist that suffering must be punishment for sin; Job protests his innocence and demands an answer from God. When God speaks out of the whirlwind, he gives no explanation but shows his wisdom and power in creation, and Job bows in trust. The book refuses easy answers to innocent suffering. The Fathers saw in Job a figure of Christ, the innocent one who suffered, and the Church reads his hope in a living Redeemer (19:25) at funerals.
JOB.author: Unknown. The Talmud named Moses; others suggested one of the prophets; and Gregory the Great held that the question mattered little, since the Holy Spirit is its author. Most scholars see a gifted Israelite poet who set a great poetic debate within an older tale of a patient man (chapters 1–2 and 42); Elihu’s speeches (32–37) may be later.
JOB.date: Uncertain; most scholars place it between the 6th and 4th centuries BC, though the story of Job is older.
JOB.language: Hebrew, in difficult poetry rich in rare words
JOB.setting: Job is not an Israelite: he lives in the land of Uz, somewhere east of Israel, in a time like that of the patriarchs, and his story could belong to any people. The book comes from Israel’s wisdom tradition, probably after the Exile, when national disaster had shaken the simple belief that God always rewards the good and punishes the wicked in this life.

key.note: “The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away”
“I know that my Redeemer liveth”: in my flesh I shall see God
God answers from the whirlwind: “Where wast thou?”
Job: “now my eye seeth thee”; he does penance in dust and ashes

sources: Gregory the Great, Moralia in Job

PSA.about: The prayer book of Israel and of the Church: 150 songs of praise, lament, thanksgiving, trust and repentance, gathered over centuries for worship. Every human feeling is brought before God here, from joy to despair. Jesus prayed the psalms, even on the cross (Psalm 22), and the apostles read them as speaking of him. The Church prays them every day in the Liturgy of the Hours and at Mass, praying them, as Saint Augustine taught, with Christ who prays in us and to Christ who is our God.
PSA.author: Tradition links the Psalter with David, and seventy-three psalms bear his name in their Hebrew titles; others are ascribed to Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon and Moses. Most scholars hold that the titles were added later and that the psalms come from many poets over many centuries, some from the time of the kings, many from after the Exile.
PSA.date: Composed over many centuries, from the time of the kings (perhaps the 10th century BC) to after the Exile; the collection was largely complete by the 2nd century BC.
PSA.language: Hebrew; the Douay-Rheims translates a Latin version made from the Greek
PSA.setting: Many psalms were sung in the temple at Jerusalem, at sacrifices, feasts and pilgrimages. Some come from the royal court and pray for the king, the Lord’s anointed; others from the grief of exile or the joy of return. Gathered into five books, perhaps echoing the five books of Moses, the Psalter became the prayer book of the synagogue, and then of Jesus and his Church.
themes: Praise of God, Creator and King

key.note: Jesus’ cry from the cross: “why hast thou forsaken me?”
“The Lord ruleth me”: the shepherd psalm
The Miserere, the great psalm of repentance
“The Lord said to my Lord”; a priest for ever like Melchizedek

PSA.canon: The Douay-Rheims and older Catholic books follow the Greek and Latin (Vulgate) numbering, which runs one lower for most psalms (Psalm 51 is their 50); the app shows it where it differs. Verse numbers here count a psalm’s title, usually as verse 1.
sources: General Instruction of the Liturgy of the Hours

PRO.about: A collection of wise sayings for living well before God: on work and laziness, speech and silence, money, friendship, marriage, the raising of children and, above all, the fear of the Lord. Its first nine chapters are a father’s instruction, in which Wisdom herself speaks, calling to the young in the streets and present with God at creation. The Church has read this Wisdom as foreshadowing Christ, the Wisdom of God, and in the liturgy applies her words to Mary. The book closes with a portrait of the valiant woman.
PRO.author: Tradition ascribes Proverbs to Solomon, famed for his wisdom, and his name heads the main collections; the book also names the men of King Hezekiah, Agur (“Gatherer” in the Douay-Rheims) and Lemuel. Most scholars think it gathers sayings from many sages over centuries, some perhaps from Solomon’s court, one section close to an Egyptian work, edited after the Exile with chapters 1–9 as an introduction.
PRO.date: Sayings from the time of the kings onward; the book probably reached its final form in the 5th or 4th century BC.
PRO.setting: Israel’s wisdom grew up at the royal court, in the schools of scribes and in the family home, where parents taught children how life works under God. It shared much with the wisdom of Egypt and Mesopotamia, but rooted it all in the fear of the Lord. Proverbs speaks to everyday life: the field, the market, the household and the city gate where justice was done.
themes: Wisdom as God’s gift and call
Family, marriage and the training of the young

key.note: The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom
Trust in the Lord with all your heart, not your own prudence
Wisdom speaks: with God from the beginning, present at creation
The valiant woman, praised because she fears the Lord

sources: Roland E. Murphy, The Tree of Life: An Exploration of Biblical Wisdom Literature

ECC.about: A restless, honest book. “Vanity of vanities”, says the Preacher: everything under the sun passes like a breath (the Hebrew word behind “vanity”): wealth, pleasure, work, even wisdom; and death comes to wise and fool alike. Yet he keeps returning to simple gifts from God’s hand (food, work, the company of those we love) and he ends: fear God and keep his commandments. The Fathers read it as a lesson in detachment from passing things, which empties the heart of false hopes and readies it for God.
ECC.author: The book calls its author Qoheleth (in Greek and Latin, Ecclesiastes), “the Preacher”, son of David and king in Jerusalem, and tradition understood this as Solomon. Most scholars, Catholic ones included, think a later sage wrote in Solomon’s person as a literary device. The epilogue (12:9–14) speaks of the Preacher in the third person and may come from a disciple.
ECC.date: Probably the 4th or 3rd century BC, judging by its late Hebrew, which includes Persian loanwords.
ECC.setting: Written probably in Judea under Persian or early Greek rule, in a settled society with wealth, officials and leisure for reflection, but also injustice and uncertainty. Israel’s hope of life beyond death was still dim. The Preacher looks hard at a life that seems to end in the grave, refuses every comfortable answer, and still holds on to God.
themes: Death and the limits of wisdom

key.note: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity”
A time for everything under heaven
Remember your Creator in the days of your youth
The conclusion: fear God and keep his commandments

sources: Roland E. Murphy, Ecclesiastes (Word Biblical Commentary)

SNG.about: A collection of love poems in which a bride and her beloved seek, lose and find each other, delighting in each other amid gardens, vineyards and spring. Read plainly, it honours the love of man and woman as God’s good gift. Jewish and Christian tradition have also read it as a song of God’s love for his people. The Fathers and mystics heard in it Christ and his Church, and Christ and the soul; the liturgy sings its verses of Mary. Near its end comes the cry that love is strong as death (8:6).
SNG.author: The title links it with Solomon, and tradition held him to be the author. Most scholars think it is a collection of love songs, perhaps by several poets, gathered later under Solomon’s name as patron of song and wisdom; some see the hand of a single poet. Rabbi Akiva called it the holiest of all the Writings.
SNG.date: Uncertain: some songs may be old, but the language suggests that the collection took its final form after the Exile, perhaps between the 5th and 3rd centuries BC.
SNG.setting: The poems breathe the life of the land of Israel: spring rain and flowering vines, shepherds and gardens, the streets of Jerusalem, with Solomon’s royal splendour in the background. Some may have been sung at weddings. God is hardly named, yet Israel received the book among its Scriptures, and Jewish custom came to read it at Passover, the feast of God’s love for his people.
themes: Christ the Bridegroom and the Church his Bride

key.note: The bride’s opening longing: “Let him kiss me”
The beloved’s call: arise, my love, for winter is past
“Thou art all fair”: sung of the Immaculate Virgin in the liturgy
Love strong as death, which many waters cannot quench

SNG.canon: Called the Canticle of Canticles in the Douay-Rheims. The title is a Hebrew way of saying “the greatest of songs”.
sources: Origen, Commentary and Homilies on the Song of Songs
Bernard of Clairvaux, Sermons on the Song of Songs
Roland E. Murphy, The Song of Songs (Hermeneia)

WIS.about: Written in Solomon’s name to the rulers of the earth, this book urges its readers to love justice and seek wisdom. It teaches that God made man for immortality and that the souls of the just are in God’s hand, praises Wisdom as the brightness of God’s eternal light, and retells the Exodus to show God saving his own. The Church reads its portrait of the just man mocked and condemned (2:12–20) as a prophecy of Christ’s Passion, and the New Testament echoes its language in speaking of Christ.
WIS.author: The writer speaks as Solomon, and some early Christians took this literally, but Jerome and Augustine already noted that it was not his. Scholars today agree that it was written by a learned Greek-speaking Jew, probably of Alexandria, who adopted Solomon’s voice as a literary convention.
WIS.date: Probably in the late 1st century BC or early 1st century AD; many think under Augustus, after Rome took Egypt in 30 BC. Likely the last Old Testament book written.
WIS.setting: Alexandria in Egypt had a large and prosperous Jewish community living amid Greek philosophy, Egyptian animal cults and the worship of rulers. Some Jews were drifting from their faith, and others were mocked for it. The author draws on Greek learning to show that the wisdom the Greeks sought is found in Israel’s God and his law, and that the faithful, though despised, will be vindicated beyond death.
themes: Immortality and the hope of the just
God’s saving judgement in the Exodus

key.note: The wicked plot against the just man, read as foretelling the Passion
The souls of the just are in the hand of God
Wisdom, brightness of eternal light and unspotted mirror of God’s majesty
The Creator known from the greatness and beauty of his creatures

WIS.canon: Also called the Wisdom of Solomon. One of the deuterocanonical books, those not in the Jewish Bible: Catholics and the Orthodox receive it as Scripture (Councils of Hippo and Carthage, 393–397; Florence, 1442; Trent, 1546); Protestants generally do not.
sources: Jerome, Preface to the Books of Solomon
David Winston, The Wisdom of Solomon (Anchor Bible)

SIR.about: A Jerusalem teacher’s counsel on almost every part of life, from friendship, speech and money to prayer, almsgiving, the honour due to parents and to physicians, and above all the fear of the Lord. Its great claim is that Wisdom has made her home in Israel and is found in the law of Moses (24:32–33). Chapters 44–50 praise Israel’s great men, from Enoch to the high priest Simon. Its Latin name, Ecclesiasticus, “the church book”, probably reflects how much the early Church used it in teaching.
SIR.author: Unusually, the author names himself: Jesus, son of Sirach, of Jerusalem (50:29), known in Hebrew as Ben Sira. His grandson translated the book into Greek in Egypt and wrote a preface, printed before chapter 1 in many Bibles. Scholars generally accept this attribution.
SIR.date: About 190–180 BC: it looks back on the high priest Simon II, who died about 200 BC, and knows nothing of the crisis after 175 BC. Translated by the grandson after 132 BC.
SIR.language: Hebrew; complete in Greek, about two-thirds of the Hebrew recovered
SIR.setting: Jerusalem around 190–180 BC, newly under the Seleucid kings of Syria, who had taken Judea from Egypt. Greek culture was drawing educated young Jews, and some thought Israel’s faith old-fashioned. Ben Sira, a scribe who taught the young, showed that Israel’s wisdom could stand beside any in the world, and urged loyalty to God’s law and to the temple and its priesthood, just before the crisis under Antiochus IV.
themes: The fear of the Lord as true wisdom

key.note: Coming to serve God: prepare for trial, and trust him
God left man in the hand of his own counsel: life or death
Wisdom’s praise: from the Most High, she makes her home in Israel
“Let us now praise men of renown”: the praise of the fathers

SIR.canon: Called Ecclesiasticus in the Douay-Rheims. One of the deuterocanonical books, those not in the Jewish Bible: Catholics and the Orthodox receive it as Scripture (Councils of Hippo and Carthage, 393–397; Florence, 1442; Trent, 1546); Protestants generally do not. Its verse numbers often differ from modern Bibles.
sources: Jerome, Preface to the Books of Solomon
Patrick W. Skehan and Alexander A. Di Lella, The Wisdom of Ben Sira (Anchor Bible)

ISA.about: The prophet most often quoted in the New Testament. Isaiah sees the Lord enthroned in holiness, calls Judah to trust in him rather than in armies and alliances, and announces both judgement and a coming king of David’s line who will bring peace. Later chapters comfort the exiles, promise salvation to the ends of the earth and portray the Servant who suffers for the sins of many. So clearly does the book speak of Christ that Saint Jerome said Isaiah should be called an evangelist rather than a prophet.
ISA.author: Tradition ascribes the whole book to Isaiah son of Amoz, a prophet in Jerusalem in the 8th century BC, and the New Testament quotes all its parts under his name. Most scholars today, Catholic ones among them, think disciples gathered and expanded his oracles, and that chapters 40–55 and 56–66 come from later prophets in his tradition, during and after the Exile.
ISA.date: Isaiah preached about 740–700 BC; chapters 40–55 probably date from about 550–539 BC, and the book reached its final form after the return from exile.
ISA.language: Hebrew; a complete scroll survives among the Dead Sea Scrolls
ISA.setting: Isaiah was called in the year King Uzziah died, about 740 BC, as Assyria was swallowing up the small kingdoms of the region. He counselled King Ahaz when Israel and Syria attacked Judah (about 734 BC), saw the northern kingdom fall in 722 BC, and stood by King Hezekiah when Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem in 701 BC. Chapters 40–55 speak to the exiles in Babylon and name Cyrus of Persia as their deliverer; the last chapters address those rebuilding Jerusalem.
themes: Trust in God, not in human power

key.note: Isaiah’s call and the seraphim’s cry: “Holy, holy, holy”
A virgin shall conceive and bear a son, Emmanuel
“A child is born to us”: the Prince of Peace
The Servant, wounded for our iniquities, led as a sheep to slaughter

sources: The Navarre Bible: Major Prophets, introduction to Isaiah
Joseph Blenkinsopp, A History of Prophecy in Israel

JER.about: The book of the prophet who had to tell his own people that Jerusalem would fall, and lived to see it. Jeremiah pleads with Judah to return to the Lord, attacks false trust in the temple, and pours out his anguish to God in prayers often called his “confessions”. Yet in the darkest hour he buys a field as a pledge of the future and promises a new covenant written on the heart (31:31–34), which the New Testament sees sealed in Christ’s blood. The Fathers saw in this innocent, persecuted prophet a figure of Christ.
JER.author: Tradition ascribes the book to Jeremiah, of a priestly family from Anathoth near Jerusalem, who dictated his oracles to his secretary Baruch and had them written again after the king burned the scroll (chapter 36). Most scholars think the book grew from such collections, from accounts of his life perhaps written by Baruch, and from later editing during the Exile.
JER.date: Jeremiah preached from about 627 BC until after the fall of Jerusalem in 587 BC; the book was edited during the Exile and perhaps later.
JER.setting: Jeremiah lived through Judah’s last forty years. He saw King Josiah’s reform, the fall of Assyria and the rise of Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar, who captured Jerusalem in 597 BC and destroyed it with its temple in 587 BC. Because he told the kings to submit to Babylon as God’s judgement, he was beaten, imprisoned and lowered into a muddy cistern as a traitor. After the city fell, fleeing Judeans took him to Egypt, and there the record of his life ends.
themes: Return to the Lord with the whole heart
A new covenant written on the heart

key.note: Jeremiah’s call: known and sanctified before he was born
The temple sermon: no false trust in “the temple of the Lord”
His anguish: the word like a fire shut up in his bones
The promise of a new covenant written on the heart

JER.canon: Called Jeremias in the Douay-Rheims. The Greek version is shorter and arranges some chapters differently, a sign that more than one edition of the book circulated.
sources: The Navarre Bible: Major Prophets, introduction to Jeremiah

LAM.about: Five poems of grief over Jerusalem, destroyed by the Babylonians with its temple. They picture the ruined city as a widow weeping alone, confess that the disaster came from the people’s sins, and still cling to the Lord, whose mercies are “new every morning” (3:23). Four of the poems are alphabetic: each verse or group of verses begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and the Douay-Rheims keeps the letters’ names. The Church has long sung them in Holy Week, hearing in them the sorrow of Christ in his Passion.
LAM.author: Greek and Latin Bibles open the book with a note that Jeremiah sat weeping over Jerusalem and spoke these laments, and tradition has long ascribed them to him. Most scholars think they come from one or more unknown poets who lived through the city’s fall, since their style and outlook differ in places from Jeremiah’s.
LAM.date: Soon after the fall of Jerusalem in 587 BC, probably before the first exiles returned in 538 BC.
LAM.setting: In 587 BC the army of Nebuchadnezzar broke through Jerusalem’s walls after a long siege. The temple was burned, the king blinded and led away, and many of the people deported to Babylon. Those left behind faced famine, ruins and the mockery of their neighbours. These poems give voice to that grief, perhaps for services of mourning held among the ruins, and Jews still read them each year on the fast that remembers the temple’s destruction.
themes: Hope in the Lord’s faithful mercy
Prayer in the midst of ruin

key.note: Jerusalem: “see if there be any sorrow like to my sorrow”
The Lord’s mercies are new every morning; it is good to wait
“Convert us, O Lord, to thee, and we shall be converted”

LAM.canon: In the Douay-Rheims, “The Lamentations of Jeremias”. Greek and Latin Bibles place it with Jeremiah; the Hebrew Bible counts it among the Writings.
sources: The Navarre Bible: Major Prophets, introduction to Lamentations

BAR.about: A short book bearing the name of Baruch, Jeremiah’s secretary, and set among the exiles in Babylon. It opens with a humble confession of the nation’s sins, praises the wisdom God gave Israel in his Law, and ends by comforting Jerusalem with the promise that her children will come home. Its sixth chapter, the Letter of Jeremiah, mocks the lifeless idols of Babylon. The Fathers read the words “afterwards he was seen upon earth, and conversed with men” (3:38) as a prophecy of the Incarnation.
BAR.author: The book names Baruch son of Neriah, writing in Babylon five years after Jerusalem was burned (1:1–2), and tradition accepted him as its author. Most scholars think it was put together much later by one or more unknown Jewish writers, who joined a prayer, a wisdom poem and a poem of consolation under the name of Jeremiah’s faithful companion. The Letter of Jeremiah is a separate work.
BAR.date: Uncertain; many scholars place the book in the 2nd or 1st century BC. The Letter of Jeremiah may be older, from between the 4th and 2nd centuries BC.
BAR.language: Survives in Greek; at least the first part was probably Hebrew
BAR.setting: The book is set among the exiles in Babylon after 587 BC, but it speaks to every generation of Jews living among foreign peoples and their gods. Its prayer confesses that Israel’s sufferings are deserved; its poem teaches that the wisdom all nations seek has been given to Israel in the Law of God; its closing poems hold out the hope of return. The Letter warns exiles not to be awed by processions of gilded idols.

key.note: “Hear, O Israel, the commandments of life”: where wisdom is found
God gives wisdom to Israel; “afterwards he was seen upon earth”
Jerusalem told to put off mourning and see her children gathered
The Letter of Jeremiah warns the exiles against worshipping idols

BAR.canon: Deuterocanonical: Catholics and the Orthodox receive it as Scripture; Protestants generally do not. The lists of Hippo and Carthage (393–397) are generally understood to include it under Jeremiah; Florence (1442) and Trent (1546) confirmed that canon, Trent naming Baruch with Jeremiah. Greek Bibles print the Letter of Jeremiah separately.
sources: Council of Trent, Decree on the Canonical Scriptures (1546)
The Navarre Bible: Major Prophets, introduction to Baruch

EZK.about: The book of a priest who became a prophet in exile. Ezekiel’s visions are among the most striking in Scripture: the glory of the Lord enthroned above living creatures and wheels, leaving the defiled temple and later returning to a new one. He acts out his messages in strange signs, teaches that each person answers for his own sins, and after Jerusalem’s fall promises a new heart and a new spirit, and that God himself will shepherd his flock. The Church hears in these promises Baptism, the gift of the Spirit and Christ the Good Shepherd.
EZK.author: Ezekiel son of Buzi, a priest deported to Babylon with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC. The book speaks mostly in his own voice and dates many of its oracles, and tradition takes it as his. Most scholars agree that the bulk of it comes from him, while disciples arranged it and added to it, especially in the closing vision of the new temple (chapters 40–48).
EZK.date: Ezekiel’s dated oracles run from 593 to 571 BC; his followers completed the book later in the Exile.
EZK.setting: Ezekiel lived among the exiles beside the river Chebar in Babylonia. Until 587 BC he told them, against their hopes, that Jerusalem would fall because of its idolatry and injustice; when a refugee brought word that it had (33:21), his message turned to hope. Far from the temple, the exiles learned that God’s glory was not confined to Jerusalem, and that he could bring a people as good as dead back to life.
themes: The glory and holiness of God
A new heart and a new spirit
The renewed temple and river of life

key.note: The vision of the glory of the Lord upon his throne
God himself will seek and shepherd his scattered sheep
Clean water, a new heart and God’s own spirit
The valley of dry bones brought back to life

sources: The Navarre Bible: Major Prophets, introduction to Ezekiel
Joseph Blenkinsopp, A History of Prophecy in Israel

DAN.about: Two kinds of writing meet in Daniel. Stories of Daniel and his three companions at the royal court in Babylon show faithful Jews refusing to worship idols and being saved from the fiery furnace and the lions’ den. Visions then reveal that the empires of the world will pass and that God will give an everlasting kingdom to “one like the Son of man” (7:13–14), the title Jesus took for himself. The book also gives one of the Old Testament’s clearest promises of the resurrection of the dead (12:2).
DAN.author: The book’s hero, and the speaker of its visions, is Daniel, a young noble taken to Babylon. Tradition, which hears Jesus speak of “Daniel the prophet” (Matthew 24:15), held that he wrote it in the 6th century BC. Most scholars today, Catholic ones among them, think an unknown author gathered older stories about Daniel and added the visions during the persecution of 167–164 BC.
DAN.date: Tradition: the 6th century BC. Most scholars: completed about 165 BC, since the visions describe the persecution under Antiochus IV in close detail; some of the stories may be older.
DAN.language: Hebrew and Aramaic (2:4–7:28); the additions survive in Greek
DAN.setting: The stories are set in the courts of Babylon and Persia in the 6th century BC, among Jews serving foreign kings. The visions look ahead to the Greek kingdoms that followed Alexander the Great, and to King Antiochus IV, who in 167 BC banned Jewish worship and set up a pagan altar in the temple, the “abomination of desolation”. To Jews facing martyrdom under Antiochus, the book taught that God rules history and that the faithful dead will rise.
themes: God rules the kingdoms of the world
The Son of man and the everlasting kingdom

key.note: The three young men call all creation to bless the Lord
Daniel in the lions’ den: “My God hath sent his angel”
One like the Son of man receives an everlasting kingdom
The dead shall awake, some to everlasting life, others to reproach

DAN.canon: The Greek additions, received by Catholics and the Orthodox but generally not by Protestants, are the Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three Young Men (3:24–90), Susanna (chapter 13) and Bel and the Dragon (chapter 14); Trent affirmed them. The Hebrew Bible places Daniel among the Writings.
sources: Council of Trent, Decree on the Canonical Scriptures (1546)
The Navarre Bible: Major Prophets, introduction to Daniel

HOS.about: The first of the twelve shorter prophetic books, called “minor” only because they are short. Hosea’s marriage to an unfaithful wife becomes a living parable: Israel has betrayed the Lord for the god Baal, yet he will not give her up, but will lead her into the wilderness, speak to her heart and espouse her to himself for ever. Few books show so tenderly that God loves as a faithful husband and a father. Jesus twice quotes its words, “I desired mercy, and not sacrifice” (6:6).
HOS.author: Hosea son of Beeri, the only prophet of the northern kingdom whose collected oracles form a book of their own. Scholars generally accept the oracles as his, gathered after Samaria fell and brought south to Judah, where they were edited and some references to Judah added.
HOS.date: Hosea preached from about 750 BC until shortly before Samaria fell in 722 BC; the book took its final shape in Judah, perhaps during or after the Exile.
HOS.language: Hebrew, in one of the Bible’s most difficult texts
HOS.setting: Hosea spoke to Israel, the northern kingdom, at the end of the prosperous reign of Jeroboam II and through the chaos that followed, when kings were murdered one after another and Assyria closed in. Many Israelites worshipped Baal, the Canaanite god of rain and fertility, alongside the Lord, or sought safety in alliances with Egypt and Assyria. Hosea warned that such unfaithfulness would end in ruin, as it did when Samaria fell in 722 BC.
themes: Mercy and the knowledge of God

key.note: God will win back his unfaithful bride and espouse her for ever
“I desired mercy, and not sacrifice”, quoted by Jesus
“I called my son out of Egypt”: God’s fatherly love
The closing call: “Return, O Israel, to the Lord thy God”

sources: The Navarre Bible: Minor Prophets, introduction to Hosea

JOL.about: A short book that begins with a plague of locusts and turns it into a summons. Joel sees the disaster as a warning of the day of the Lord and calls everyone, priests and people, to fast and to “rend your hearts, and not your garments” (2:13), words the Church reads on Ash Wednesday. God answers with rain and plenty, and with a greater promise: he will pour out his spirit upon all flesh. Saint Peter proclaimed that promise fulfilled on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:16–21).
JOL.author: Joel son of Pethuel, of whom nothing else is known. His close concern for the temple, its priests and its offerings suggests that he lived in Jerusalem, and some scholars think he spoke within the temple’s worship.
JOL.date: Uncertain. Older writers placed it early, some in the 9th century BC; most scholars now date it after the Exile, perhaps about 400 BC, since it names no king and assumes a working temple.
JOL.setting: The book gives few clues to its time. No king is mentioned: Judah is led by priests and elders, and the temple’s daily offerings go on, which fits the period after the Exile. Then a plague of locusts and a drought strip the land and halt the offerings. Joel reads this disaster as a sign and calls a solemn fast, then widens his gaze to the judgement of the nations that scattered God’s people.

key.note: “Rend your hearts, and not your garments”: the call to conversion
God pours out his spirit; all who call on his name are saved
The nations summoned to judgement in the valley of Josaphat

JOL.canon: Some modern Bibles, following the Hebrew, have four chapters: there the Douay-Rheims 2:28–32 is 3:1–5, and its chapter 3 is chapter 4.
sources: The Navarre Bible: Minor Prophets, introduction to Joel

AMO.about: Probably the earliest of the prophets whose words fill a book of their own. Amos, a herdsman from Judah, went north to the royal shrine of Bethel and condemned a prosperous Israel for selling “the poor man for a pair of shoes” (2:6) while keeping splendid feasts. God, he said, rejects the worship of those who trample the poor; he wants justice to flow like a mighty torrent. The book ends with the promise that God will raise up the fallen tent of David, which the apostles saw fulfilled as Gentiles entered the Church (Acts 15:16–17).
AMO.author: Amos of Tekoa, a herdsman and gatherer of wild figs who insisted he was no professional prophet (7:14–15). Most scholars hold that the bulk of the book preserves his words, gathered by disciples, with later additions such as the short hymns of praise and, many think, the hopeful ending (9:11–15).
AMO.date: Amos preached about 760–750 BC, “two years before the earthquake” (1:1); the book was edited in Judah, with some passages probably added during or after the Exile.
AMO.setting: Under Jeroboam II, the northern kingdom of Israel enjoyed a time of peace and prosperity. The rich built houses of ivory and feasted, while the poor were cheated with false weights, sold for debt and denied justice in the courts. Festivals at the shrines of Bethel and Gilgal flourished. Into this confident society came Amos, an outsider from Judah, to announce that the day of the Lord would be darkness, not light, and that Israel would go into exile.

key.note: God rejects feasts without justice: let justice flow like a torrent
Amos: no prophet by trade, but sent by the Lord
A famine not of bread, but of hearing the word of the Lord
God will raise up the fallen tabernacle of David

sources: The Navarre Bible: Minor Prophets, introduction to Amos
Joseph Blenkinsopp, A History of Prophecy in Israel

OBA.about: The shortest book of the Old Testament, a single chapter of 21 verses. It condemns Edom, the neighbouring nation descended from Esau, Jacob’s brother, for gloating, looting and cutting off fugitives when Jerusalem fell. Edom’s pride will be brought low: “as thou hast done, so shall it be done to thee” (verse 15). The book ends with the day of the Lord, when Mount Zion will be saved and “the kingdom shall be for the Lord”, a hope Christians see fulfilled in the kingdom of God that Christ proclaimed.
OBA.author: Nothing is known of Obadiah beyond his name, which means “servant of the Lord”. An old Jewish tradition identified him with the Obadiah who hid the Lord’s prophets from Jezebel (1 Kings 18), but the book itself speaks of a much later time.
OBA.date: Probably soon after the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem in 587 BC, since it describes Edom’s part in that disaster.
OBA.setting: Edom lay south-east of the Dead Sea, and Israel never forgot that its people descended from Esau, Jacob’s twin. When the Babylonians sacked Jerusalem in 587 BC, the Edomites joined in the plunder and later moved into southern Judah, a betrayal remembered bitterly in Psalm 137 and in Lamentations. Its opening verses closely resemble parts of Jeremiah 49:7–22: either one borrows from the other, or both draw on an older oracle against Edom.
themes: God judges cruelty to a brother

key.note: Edom’s pride: though nested among the stars, it will be brought down
Edom’s guilt: violence against his brother Jacob in his day of ruin
“As thou hast done, so shall it be done to thee”
Saviours on Mount Sion: “the kingdom shall be for the Lord”

sources: The Navarre Bible: Minor Prophets, introduction to Obadiah

JON.about: Unlike the other prophetic books, Jonah is a story about a prophet rather than a collection of his sayings. Sent to preach in Nineveh, a great city of Assyria, Israel’s cruel enemy, Jonah runs the other way, is swallowed by a great fish, and at last preaches, only to sulk when the city repents and God spares it. The book’s point is God’s mercy, which reaches even Israel’s enemies. Jesus made Jonah’s three days in the fish a sign of his own death and resurrection (Matthew 12:40).
JON.author: The hero is Jonah son of Amittai, a prophet in the reign of Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25), and tradition long read the book as a historical account of his mission. Most scholars today, Catholic ones among them, read it as an inspired teaching story, akin to a parable, by an unknown author after the Exile. Either way its message is the same.
JON.date: Set in the 8th century BC; most scholars date the writing after the Exile, often to the 5th or 4th century BC, judging by its late Hebrew and distant memory of Nineveh.
JON.setting: Nineveh, a great city of Assyria and later its capital, stood for the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BC, remembered for its cruelty until the city fell in 612 BC. If, as most think, the book was written after the Exile, it spoke to a community tempted to close in on itself and wish judgement on the nations. Jonah’s anger mirrors theirs, and God’s closing question (4:11) is left for the reader to answer.

key.note: Jonah flees from God’s call, taking ship for Tharsis
Three days in the fish, and Jonah’s prayer from the depths
Nineveh repents in sackcloth, and God spares it
“Shall I not spare Ninive?”: God’s compassion for the city

JON.canon: Called Jonas in the Douay-Rheims, where the great fish comes at 2:1 (1:17 in many English Bibles).
sources: The Navarre Bible: Minor Prophets, introduction to Jonah

MIC.about: Micah, a countryman from the foothills of Judah, speaks for the poor against those who seize their fields and against rulers, priests and prophets who sell justice. He dared to say that Jerusalem itself would be ploughed like a field. Yet his book also holds great hopes: nations streaming to the Lord’s mountain to learn peace, and a ruler from little Bethlehem, a prophecy Matthew’s Gospel sees fulfilled in the birth of Jesus. God’s plea “O my people, what have I done to thee?” (6:3) is sung in the Reproaches of Good Friday.
MIC.author: Micah of Moresheth, a contemporary of Isaiah, whose warning against Jerusalem was still remembered a century later (Jeremiah 26:18). Most scholars think chapters 1–3 are largely his, while many of the promises in chapters 4–7 were added by later hands during or after the Exile; others defend more of the book as his.
MIC.date: Micah preached about 735–700 BC; the book was completed later, probably during or after the Exile.
MIC.setting: Micah preached under Kings Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, as Assyria destroyed Samaria (722 BC) and then ravaged the towns of Judah’s foothills, the region of his own home, in 701 BC. Meanwhile powerful landowners and officials tied to Jerusalem’s court were swallowing up small family farms. Micah saw both the Assyrian armies and this injustice as signs of judgement, and called the nation’s leaders back to the covenant.

key.note: Nations stream to the Lord’s mountain; swords beaten into ploughshares
From Bethlehem Ephrata shall come the ruler in Israel
“O my people, what have I done to thee?” and what God asks
Who is a God like thee, casting our sins into the sea?

sources: The Navarre Bible: Minor Prophets, introduction to Micah
Joseph Blenkinsopp, A History of Prophecy in Israel
