NAM.about: A poem of triumph over the fall of Nineveh, capital of Assyria, the empire that had terrorised the Near East for more than a century. Nahum, whose name means “comfort”, opens with a hymn to the Lord, patient yet just, who will not acquit the guilty, and then pictures the city’s fall in vivid scenes of battle. To the oppressed it brings comfort: God sees, and tyranny does not have the last word. Its herald on the mountains “that bringeth good tidings” (1:15) matches words of Isaiah (52:7) that Saint Paul applies to preachers of the Gospel.
NAM.author: Nahum the Elkoshite, from a place called Elkosh that has never been identified with certainty. Nothing else is known of him. Scholars generally accept the oracles as his, perhaps later arranged for use in worship.
NAM.date: Between the sack of Thebes in Egypt in 663 BC, recalled in 3:8 (“Alexandria” in the Douay-Rheims), and the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC, perhaps nearer the end.
NAM.setting: For more than a century Assyria dominated the region by brutal force: it destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BC, ravaged Judah in 701 BC and made its kings pay tribute. By the late 7th century BC its power was crumbling, and in 612 BC Nineveh fell to the Babylonians and the Medes. Nahum announces that fall to a Judah that had long suffered under Assyrian rule.
themes: The Lord, slow to anger yet just

key.note: “The Lord is good, and giveth strength in the day of trouble”
On the mountains, the feet of him who brings good tidings of peace
Woe to the city of blood: Nineveh is laid waste

sources: The Navarre Bible: Minor Prophets, introduction to Nahum

HAB.about: Habakkuk does what few prophets do: he questions God aloud. Why does the Lord let violence and injustice go unpunished? And when God answers that he is raising up the Babylonians (the “Chaldeans”), why should the wicked devour those more just than themselves? God’s reply is to wait for the vision and trust: “the just shall live in his faith” (2:4), words Saint Paul made central to his teaching on faith. The book ends with a psalm that rejoices in God even when every harvest fails.
HAB.author: Nothing is known of Habakkuk but his name and his title of prophet. The psalm-like heading and closing note of his prayer (chapter 3) lead some scholars to think he served in the temple’s worship; others think that prayer was added from another source. A story among the Greek additions to Daniel (14:32–38) has him carrying a meal to Daniel in the lions’ den.
HAB.date: Probably about 605–597 BC, after Babylon had defeated Egypt and before it first captured Jerusalem; some date it a little earlier.
HAB.setting: In Judah, probably under King Jehoiakim, the powerful oppressed the weak and the law went unenforced. Abroad, Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar crushed Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC and became master of the region. Habakkuk wrestles with both evils: the violence within his own people, and the cruelty of the empire God was raising up to punish it. The answer he receives is not an explanation but a call to faithful waiting.
themes: The just shall live by faith
Joy in God when all else fails

key.note: “How long, O Lord, shall I cry?”: the prophet’s complaint
Wait for the vision: “the just shall live in his faith”
“The Lord is in his holy temple”: let all the earth keep silence
Though every harvest fails, “I will rejoice in the Lord”

sources: The Navarre Bible: Minor Prophets, introduction to Habakkuk

ZEP.about: Zephaniah proclaims the day of the Lord as a day of wrath for Judah and the nations, a warning so stark that its Latin words, “Dies irae, dies illa” (1:15), became the opening of a famous medieval hymn on the Last Judgement. Yet he also tells the humble to seek the Lord, promises a remnant of the poor who hope in his name, and ends with a song of joy: the Lord is in the midst of the daughter of Zion. The Church reads that song in Advent and on the feast of the Visitation, applying it to Mary.
ZEP.author: Zephaniah son of Cushi, whose descent is traced back four generations to a Hezekiah, perhaps the king (1:1). Most scholars accept the core of the book as his, with some later additions, especially among the promises of the last chapter.
ZEP.date: In the reign of King Josiah (640–609 BC), probably before his reform of 622 BC, since idol worship still flourishes in Jerusalem.
ZEP.setting: King Manasseh’s long reign had filled Jerusalem with the worship of Baal and of the stars and kept Judah a loyal vassal of Assyria. Now the young King Josiah was on the throne, Assyria was weakening, and in 622 BC Josiah would purge the land of idols. Zephaniah’s preaching, aimed at officials, merchants and the complacent who said that the Lord does nothing, may have helped prepare the way for that reform.
themes: The faithful remnant of the poor
Joy at God’s presence among his people

key.note: The great day of the Lord: “a day of wrath”
“Seek the Lord, all ye meek of the earth”
A poor and needy people left to hope in the Lord
“Give praise, O daughter of Sion”: the Lord is in thy midst

sources: The Navarre Bible: Minor Prophets, introduction to Zephaniah
Lectionary for Mass (Advent; feast of the Visitation)

HAG.about: Two short chapters with one urgent message: rebuild the house of God. The returned exiles were living in panelled houses while the temple lay in ruins, and their harvests kept failing. Haggai tells them their priorities are wrong, and within a month the work begins. To builders disheartened by the modest new temple he promises that its glory will be greater than the first. The Latin reads “the desired of all nations shall come” (2:8), words long taken of Christ, who would one day enter that temple.
HAG.author: Haggai, a prophet named with Zechariah in the book of Ezra (5:1; 6:14) as urging on the rebuilding. The book speaks of him in the third person, so it was probably put together by a disciple or editor soon after his preaching.
HAG.date: His four dated messages fall between August and December 520 BC; the book was probably compiled before the temple was completed in 515 BC.
HAG.setting: In 538 BC Cyrus of Persia allowed the Jews to return from Babylon, but the first efforts to rebuild the temple stalled amid poverty, poor harvests and opposition from neighbours. Eighteen years later, in the second year of King Darius I, the governor Zerubbabel, a descendant of David, and the high priest Joshua led a small, struggling community. Haggai roused them, and the temple was finished in 515 BC.
themes: The glory of the new temple

key.note: “Is it time for you to dwell in ceiled houses?”
“The desired of all nations shall come”, long read of the Messiah
The glory of this house shall be greater than the first
Zerubbabel, God’s chosen servant, made like a signet ring

HAG.canon: Called Aggeus in the Douay-Rheims, where Zerubbabel and the high priest Joshua appear as Zorobabel and “Jesus the son of Josedec”.
sources: The Navarre Bible: Minor Prophets, introduction to Haggai

ZEC.about: A book of two parts. In the first (chapters 1–8), night visions of horsemen, a golden lampstand and a flying scroll encourage the returned exiles to rebuild the temple and promise that God will dwell among them. The second (chapters 9–14) looks to a coming king and the last days. The Gospels draw on it again and again in telling of Christ’s Passion: the humble king riding on an ass, the thirty pieces of silver, the one whom they have pierced, the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered.
ZEC.author: Zechariah son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, probably of a priestly family, who worked alongside Haggai (Ezra 5:1). Chapters 1–8 are generally accepted as his. Because chapters 9–14 differ in style, carry no dates and seem to reflect later times, most scholars attribute them to one or more later prophets, often called “Second Zechariah”.
ZEC.date: Chapters 1–8: 520–518 BC, as their dates show. Chapters 9–14: uncertain; most date them to the 5th or 4th century BC, though some think parts are older.
ZEC.setting: Like Haggai, Zechariah spoke to the small community that had returned from exile, discouraged by poverty and by the slow rebuilding of the temple under the governor Zerubbabel and the high priest Joshua. His visions assure them that God has not forgotten Jerusalem and will cleanse his people. The later chapters address a people still waiting under foreign rule, failed by its leaders, and hoping for God’s final victory.
themes: God comes to dwell with his people
“Turn ye to me”: the call to conversion
The humble king who brings peace
The pierced one and the struck shepherd
The Lord, king over all the earth

key.note: Sing and rejoice, daughter of Sion: the Lord comes to dwell in her midst
Your king comes, just and saviour, poor and riding upon an ass
“They shall look upon me, whom they have pierced”
“Strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered”

ZEC.canon: Called Zacharias in the Douay-Rheims, where the high priest Joshua appears as “Jesus the son of Josedec” and the messianic title “Branch” as “the Orient”.
sources: The Navarre Bible: Minor Prophets, introduction to Zechariah
Joseph Blenkinsopp, A History of Prophecy in Israel

MAL.about: The last of the prophets in Christian Bibles, and a bridge to the New Testament. In a series of disputes with his hearers, Malachi rebukes priests who offer blemished sacrifices and husbands who abandon the wives of their youth, and promises that the Lord will come suddenly to his temple, preceded by his messenger. The Council of Trent saw in the “clean oblation” offered to God’s name among the nations “in every place” (1:11) a prophecy of the Mass. The book closes with the promise of Elijah, fulfilled, Jesus says, in John the Baptist.
MAL.author: The name Malachi means “my messenger” (compare 3:1) and may be a title rather than a personal name; the Greek translation of 1:1 reads “by the hand of his messenger”. One Jewish tradition identified the author with Ezra. Nothing else is known of him.
MAL.date: Probably about 500–450 BC: the temple has been rebuilt (515 BC), but the abuses he attacks are those that Ezra and Nehemiah later tried to reform.
MAL.setting: Decades after the temple was rebuilt, the first enthusiasm had faded. Judah was a small province of the Persian Empire under a governor. Priests grew careless, offering sick and lame animals; people held back their tithes; some men married women who worshipped other gods and divorced the wives of their youth. Many asked whether serving God was worth it. Malachi answers that God still loves Israel and will come to purify and to heal.
themes: Worship offered with a pure heart
The messenger who prepares the way

key.note: A clean oblation offered to God’s name among the nations
The messenger prepares the way; the Lord comes to his temple
“The Sun of justice shall arise, and health in his wings”
God will send Elijah before the great day of the Lord

MAL.canon: Called Malachias in the Douay-Rheims. Bibles that follow the Hebrew have three chapters, numbering 4:1–6 as 3:19–24.
sources: Council of Trent, Session 22, Doctrine on the Sacrifice of the Mass, chapter 1
The Navarre Bible: Minor Prophets, introduction to Malachi

MAT.about: The Gospel that stands first in the New Testament, and the one the early Church quoted most. Written for believers steeped in the Jewish Scriptures, it presents Jesus as the Messiah, son of David and son of Abraham, in whom the Law and the Prophets are fulfilled. His teaching is gathered into five great discourses, beginning with the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7). Matthew alone among the Gospels speaks of the “church”, built on Peter (16:18). It begins by naming Jesus Emmanuel, “God with us” (1:23), and ends with the risen Lord’s promise to be with his disciples all days (28:20).
MAT.author: Tradition names Matthew, the tax collector who became one of the Twelve (9:9). Papias, in the early second century, says Matthew compiled the Lord’s sayings in Hebrew, and Irenaeus that he wrote a Gospel among the Hebrews. Most scholars think our Greek Gospel draws on Mark and on a collection of Jesus’ sayings, and see its author as a learned Jewish Christian, perhaps of a community that honoured Matthew.
MAT.date: Most scholars date it about AD 80–90, after the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70; tradition held it to be the first Gospel written, and some scholars still date it before 70.
MAT.language: Greek. Early writers mention a Hebrew or Aramaic Matthew; none survives.
MAT.setting: Probably written in Syria, perhaps at Antioch, for a church of Jewish and Gentile believers in the years after the Romans destroyed the Temple. Judaism was regrouping under the rabbis, heirs of the Pharisees, and church and synagogue were painfully parting ways; the Gospel’s sharp words against the scribes and Pharisees probably reflect that quarrel. Matthew shows Jesus as a new Moses teaching on the mountain, and his Church as heir to Israel’s promises, now opened to all nations.
themes: Jesus the Messiah fulfils the Scriptures
The Sermon on the Mount, the New Law

key.note: The Beatitudes, opening the Sermon on the Mount
The Our Father, the prayer Jesus taught
Thou art Peter: the rock of the Church and the keys of the kingdom
The risen Lord sends the apostles to teach and baptise all nations

sources: Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to Matthew

MRK.about: The shortest Gospel and, most scholars think, the first written. Mark tells the good news at speed: Jesus the Son of God preaching, healing and casting out demons, misunderstood even by his disciples, and going to the cross. Its turning point is Peter’s confession that Jesus is the Christ (8:29), after which Jesus teaches that the Son of Man must suffer. It is the Gospel of the cross and of discipleship as following him.
MRK.author: From the early second century (Papias, quoted by Eusebius), tradition has held that Mark, the companion of Peter and of Paul, wrote down Peter’s preaching in Rome. Many scholars accept a link with Mark and with Peter’s circle; others leave the author unknown.
MRK.date: Probably about AD 65–70, around the time of Nero’s persecution and the Jewish War.
MRK.setting: Written most likely for Christians in Rome who had seen Peter and Paul put to death and their brothers and sisters suffer under Nero. It explains Jewish customs for Gentile readers and keeps a few of Jesus’ Aramaic words. It asks what it means to follow a crucified Messiah when following him costs everything.

key.note: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God
Peter confesses that Jesus is the Christ
The Son of Man came to give his life a ransom
The centurion: Indeed this man was the son of God

MRK.canon: The ending, 16:9–20, is missing from the earliest Greek manuscripts but is received by the Church as inspired and canonical (Council of Trent).
sources: Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to Mark

LUK.about: The first part of a two-volume work completed by Acts, and the longest book of the New Testament. Luke writes an orderly account (1:1–4) of Jesus as Saviour of all, with a special tenderness for the poor, sinners, women and outsiders. Only Luke tells of the Annunciation and the Visitation and gives the three canticles the Church prays every day: the Benedictus, the Magnificat and the Nunc Dimittis. Only Luke has the parables of the good Samaritan and the prodigal son. It is a Gospel of mercy, prayer, the Holy Spirit and joy.
LUK.author: Tradition, from Irenaeus (about AD 180) onwards, names Luke, “the most dear physician” and companion of Paul (Colossians 4:14), who also wrote Acts. He was not an eyewitness, and says he drew on those who were (1:2). Many scholars accept Luke as the author; others think of an unknown, educated Christian of the next generation who admired Paul.
LUK.date: Probably about AD 80–90, since Luke uses Mark; some date it to the early 60s, because Acts, written after it, ends with Paul still alive in Rome.
LUK.language: Greek, the most literary of the four Gospels
LUK.setting: Written for “most excellent Theophilus” (1:3), perhaps a patron or official, and for Gentile Christians across the Roman world; where it was written is unknown. Luke sets the birth and preaching of Jesus within world history, under Augustus and Tiberius (2:1; 3:1), and shows Israel’s hopes fulfilled in a Saviour for every nation. Much of the Gospel follows Jesus on his long journey to Jerusalem (9:51), the city where salvation is accomplished and from which it goes out.
themes: God’s mercy for sinners and the lost
Mary, the believing handmaid of the Lord

key.note: The Annunciation: “Hail, full of grace”
The Magnificat, Mary’s song of praise
The parable of the prodigal son and the merciful father
Emmaus: the risen Lord known in the breaking of bread

LUK.canon: The angel and the sweat like drops of blood in the agony (22:43–44) are missing from some early manuscripts but are received by the Church as inspired and canonical (Council of Trent).
sources: General Instruction of the Liturgy of the Hours
Joseph Fitzmyer, The Gospel According to Luke (Anchor Bible), introduction
Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Canon of the New Testament”
Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to Luke

JHN.about: The fourth Gospel is unlike the other three. It begins before time, with the Word who was God and was made flesh (1:14). It tells fewer miracles, calling them signs, and gives long discourses in which Jesus reveals who he is: the bread of life, the light of the world, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life. From it the Church has drawn much of her teaching on the Trinity, the Incarnation, the Eucharist and the Holy Spirit. Its climax is Thomas’s confession, “My Lord and my God” (20:28), and it says it was written that we may believe and have life (20:31).
JHN.author: Tradition, from Irenaeus (about AD 180), holds that John the apostle, “the disciple whom Jesus loved” (13:23), wrote it at Ephesus in old age. The Gospel rests on that disciple’s witness, and a closing note adds, “we know that his testimony is true” (21:24). Many scholars think it took shape over time in a community formed by him, and debate whether he was John the son of Zebedee.
JHN.date: Probably about AD 90–100, the last of the four Gospels, though it preserves early memories, especially of Jerusalem and Judea.
JHN.language: Greek, simple in words and deep in meaning
JHN.setting: Tradition places it at Ephesus, among the churches of Asia Minor, at the close of the apostolic age. Its first readers seem to have been put out of the synagogue for confessing Jesus as the Christ (9:22; 16:2). Its harsh words about “the Jews” probably reflect that bitter conflict, and the Church teaches that they must not be turned against the Jewish people. The readers already knew the story of Jesus; John leads them deeper, to see his glory and abide in him.

key.note: The Prologue: the Word was God, and the Word was made flesh
God so loved the world as to give his only Son
The bread of life: except you eat his flesh and drink his blood
From the cross Jesus gives his mother to the beloved disciple

JHN.canon: The account of the woman taken in adultery (7:53–8:11) is missing from the earliest Greek manuscripts but is received by the Church as inspired and canonical (Council of Trent).
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Canon of the New Testament”
Raymond Brown, The Gospel According to John (Anchor Bible), introduction
Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to John

ACT.about: The second volume of Luke’s work, telling how the risen Lord kept his promise: the Holy Spirit came at Pentecost, and the apostles carried the gospel from Jerusalem through Judea and Samaria towards the ends of the earth (1:8). The first half follows Peter and the church in Jerusalem; the second follows Paul on his journeys, ending with him preaching in Rome. Along the way the Church prays, breaks bread, suffers, and in council at Jerusalem (chapter 15) welcomes Gentiles without requiring circumcision. It is the story of the Church’s birth.
ACT.author: The same writer as the third Gospel, addressing the same Theophilus (1:1). Tradition names Luke, Paul’s companion. In some passages the narrator says “we” (from 16:10), suggesting he travelled with Paul, though some think he drew on another’s travel diary. Many scholars accept Luke as author; others see a later admirer of Paul whose portrait of him differs somewhat from Paul’s own letters.
ACT.date: Probably about AD 80–90, after Luke’s Gospel. Some date it about AD 62–64, because it ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome, before his trial and death.
ACT.setting: Acts covers about thirty years, from the Ascension (around AD 30) to Paul’s arrival in Rome (around AD 60). Roman roads, sea lanes, a common Greek tongue and Jewish synagogues across the Empire carried the gospel. The young Church met opposition from some Jewish leaders and from pagans whose trade or worship it upset, while Roman officials often found the Christians guilty of no crime. Its great question was whether Gentile believers must keep the Law of Moses.
themes: The Holy Spirit guiding the Church
Witness to the ends of the earth
The gospel opened to the Gentiles
The life of the first Christian community

key.note: The plan of the book: witnesses to the uttermost part of the earth
Pentecost: the Holy Spirit comes upon the disciples
The first Christians: apostles’ teaching, breaking of bread, prayers
Saul meets the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus

sources: Joseph Fitzmyer, The Acts of the Apostles (Anchor Bible), introduction
Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to Acts

ROM.about: Paul’s longest letter and the fullest statement of his gospel: the power of God for the salvation of all who believe, Jew and Gentile alike (1:16). All have sinned, and all who believe are justified freely by God’s grace through faith in Christ (3:22–24). Paul sets Adam beside Christ, explains baptism as dying and rising with him, and describes life in the Spirit as God’s children (chapters 5–8). He wrestles with Israel’s place in God’s plan (9–11) and ends with the life of charity. It has shaped the Church’s teaching on original sin, grace and justification.
ROM.author: Paul; scholars do not dispute it. He dictated the letter to a secretary, Tertius, who adds his own greeting near the end (16:22).
ROM.date: About AD 56–58, from Corinth, as Paul prepared to take a collection for the poor of Jerusalem (15:25–26) before travelling on to Rome and Spain.
ROM.setting: Paul had neither founded nor yet visited the church in Rome (1:13), which had grown up among Jews and Gentiles in the capital. The emperor Claudius had expelled Jews from Rome, probably around AD 49 (Acts 18:2), and after their return Jewish and Gentile believers seem to have struggled to live as one. Paul hoped to visit on his way to Spain (15:24) and wanted their support, so he set out his gospel carefully, answering objections as he went.
themes: The gospel, God’s power to save
Life in the Spirit as God’s children

key.note: The gospel, the power of God to save all who believe
All have sinned and are justified freely by his grace
Through one man sin and death entered the world
Nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ

sources: Council of Trent, Decree on Original Sin (1546)
Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to Romans

1CO.about: A letter to a gifted, quarrelsome young church. Paul takes up its problems one by one: factions around favourite preachers, a case of incest, lawsuits, marriage and virginity, food offered to idols, disorder at the Lord’s Supper, rivalry over spiritual gifts, and doubts about the resurrection. To each he brings Christ crucified. Here are the earliest written account of the institution of the Eucharist (11:23–26), the hymn to charity (chapter 13) and the oldest list of witnesses to the risen Christ (15:3–8).
1CO.author: Paul, writing with Sosthenes (1:1); its authorship is undisputed. It mentions an earlier letter of Paul’s, now lost (5:9), and answers questions the Corinthians had sent him (7:1).
1CO.date: About AD 54–56, from Ephesus (16:8), during Paul’s long stay there.
1CO.setting: Corinth, refounded by Julius Caesar as a Roman colony in 44 BC, was a rich, crowded city on the isthmus joining mainland Greece to the Peloponnese, with a port on each sea. Paul founded the church there around AD 50–52 and stayed eighteen months (Acts 18:11). Its members were mostly Gentile converts, few of them wealthy or powerful (1:26). After he left, rival groups formed, and some, proud of their wisdom and gifts, despised weaker members and lived as if the body did not matter.
themes: Christ crucified, the wisdom of God
The Church, one body in Christ

key.note: The institution of the Eucharist, as Paul received and handed it on
Many members, one body: you are the body of Christ
The hymn to charity: the greatest of these is charity
Christ died, was buried, rose again, and was seen by many

sources: Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to 1 Corinthians

2CO.about: Paul’s most personal letter, written to a church that had hurt him. He defends his ministry against rival preachers who boasted of their credentials, and answers not with his successes but with his weakness and sufferings, through which Christ’s power shines (12:9). He speaks of the glory of God seen in the face of Christ (4:6), of the ministry of reconciliation entrusted to the apostles (5:18–20), and of generous giving to the poor of Jerusalem (chapters 8–9). Its closing blessing (13:13) is used as a greeting at Mass.
2CO.author: Paul, with Timothy (1:1); its authorship is undisputed. Many scholars think the letter as we have it joins two or more of Paul’s letters to Corinth: chapters 10–13, sharper in tone, may be a separate letter, perhaps the “tearful letter” he mentions (2:4). Others defend its unity.
2CO.date: About AD 55–57, from Macedonia (7:5), some months after 1 Corinthians; if it joins several letters, they were written within a year or two of each other.
2CO.setting: After 1 Corinthians, things went badly. Paul made a painful visit (2:1), then wrote a letter “with many tears” (2:4). Titus brought him better news in Macedonia (7:6–7), but rival missionaries had arrived in Corinth, proud of their Jewish pedigree and letters of recommendation, and scornful of Paul’s weak presence and plain speech (10:10). He answers by boasting of his weakness and sufferings for Christ, and asks the Corinthians to complete their collection for the church in Jerusalem.
themes: God’s power made perfect in weakness
The true marks of an apostle

key.note: Treasure in earthen vessels: the power is God’s, not ours
A new creature in Christ; the ministry of reconciliation
My grace is sufficient for thee: power made perfect in weakness
The Trinitarian blessing, used as a greeting at Mass

sources: The Roman Missal, Order of Mass (Greeting)
Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to 2 Corinthians

GAL.about: Paul’s most urgent letter, written in alarm and without his usual thanksgiving (1:6). Teachers had told his Gentile converts that to belong fully to God’s people they must be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses. Paul answers that we are justified not by the works of the Law but by faith in Christ (2:16), and that God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying “Abba, Father” (4:6). Christian freedom is not licence: what counts is “faith that worketh by charity” (5:6), bearing the fruit of the Spirit.
GAL.author: Paul; its authorship is undisputed. He tells his own story at length: his zeal for the Law, his call, his dealings with Peter and James, and his clash with Peter at Antioch (1:13–2:14). He closes the letter in his own hand (6:11).
GAL.date: Probably about AD 54–57, from Ephesus or Macedonia. Some scholars date it as early as AD 48–49, which would make it Paul’s earliest surviving letter.
GAL.setting: Galatia lay in the highlands of central Asia Minor (modern Turkey), named after Celtic tribes who had settled there in the third century BC; the Roman province also took in cities further south, which Paul visited in Acts 13–14. Which churches he wrote to is debated. After he left, other Christian missionaries arrived insisting on circumcision and questioning his authority. Paul answers with heat and tenderness, as a mother in labour until Christ be formed in them (4:19).
themes: Freedom from the yoke of the Law

key.note: I live, now not I: but Christ liveth in me
God sent his Son, made of a woman, that we might be sons
What avails is faith that works through charity
The fruit of the Spirit, twelve in the Church’s traditional list

sources: Council of Trent, Decree on Justification (1547), chapter 7
Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to Galatians

EPH.about: A majestic letter, more hymn and prayer than argument. It opens by blessing God for his hidden plan to gather up all things in Christ (1:10). We are saved by grace through faith (2:8), and Jews and Gentiles are made one household, built on the apostles and prophets (2:19–20). The Church is Christ’s body and his bride, one in “one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (4:5). The Church draws on it for her teaching about herself and about marriage, which the letter calls “a great sacrament” (in Greek, “mystery”) of Christ and the Church (5:32).
EPH.author: The letter names Paul, writing from prison (3:1), and the Church has received it as his since the second century; Irenaeus quotes it as Paul’s. Many, probably most, scholars today think a disciple wrote it in his name after his death, pointing to its style, its developed teaching on the Church and its close reliance on Colossians. Others hold that Paul wrote it, perhaps through a secretary.
EPH.date: If by Paul, about AD 60–62, during his imprisonment in Rome; if by a disciple, probably about AD 80–100.
EPH.setting: The words “at Ephesus” (1:1) are missing from the oldest manuscripts, and the letter has few personal touches, so it was probably meant to circulate among several churches of Asia Minor, Ephesus among them. Ephesus was the great city of the province of Asia, where Paul had worked for nearly three years (Acts 20:31). The readers were Gentile converts (2:11), learning that they now belonged with Jewish believers to one people of God.
themes: God’s plan to unite all things in Christ
The Church, body and bride of Christ

key.note: The great blessing: chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world
By grace you are saved through faith, for good works
One body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism
Husbands and wives: a great sacrament of Christ and the Church

sources: Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to Ephesians

PHP.about: The letter of joy. Written from prison, with death a real possibility, it still says again and again, “rejoice” (4:4). Paul thanks the Philippians for their gifts and long partnership in the gospel, and urges them to be of one mind in humility. At its heart is the hymn to Christ, who emptied himself, became obedient unto death on a cross, and was exalted above every name (2:5–11); the Church prays it every Saturday evening, at Evening Prayer for Sunday, and hears it on Palm Sunday. Paul counts all else loss for Christ (3:8).
PHP.author: Paul, with Timothy (1:1); its authorship is undisputed. Some scholars think it gathers two or three short letters Paul sent to Philippi, since chapter 3 changes tone abruptly (3:2); many others defend its unity.
PHP.date: It depends on where Paul was imprisoned: in Rome about AD 61–63, as tradition holds, or, as many scholars think, at Ephesus about AD 54–56.
PHP.setting: Philippi, in Macedonia (northern Greece), was a Roman colony settled with army veterans after the battle fought there in 42 BC. It was the first church Paul founded in Europe, around AD 49–50 (Acts 16), and it alone supported him from the start (4:15–16). Now he was in chains, and they had sent Epaphroditus with gifts (4:18). Paul writes to thank them, to heal their rivalries and to warn them against teachers urging circumcision.
themes: Joy in the Lord in every circumstance
The humility of Christ who emptied himself

key.note: For me, to live is Christ and to die is gain
The hymn of Christ who emptied himself and was exalted
All things counted loss for the knowledge of Christ
Rejoice in the Lord always; the peace of God guards your hearts

sources: The Liturgy of the Hours, Psalter (Evening Prayer I of Sunday)
Lectionary for Mass, Palm Sunday of the Passion of the Lord
Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to Philippians

COL.about: A letter to a church Paul had never visited (2:1), warning it against a “philosophy” (2:8) that added rules about food and feast days and a “religion of angels” (2:18) to faith in Christ. The letter answers by lifting up Christ: the image of the invisible God, in whom all things were created and hold together, head of his body, the Church (1:15–20), in whom all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily (2:9). Buried and raised with him in baptism (2:12), Christians are to seek the things that are above (3:1).
COL.author: The letter names Paul and Timothy (1:1) and closes in Paul’s own hand from prison (4:18); the Church has received it as his since the second century. Scholars are divided. Many think a disciple wrote it soon after his death, because its style and its picture of Christ as head of the Church differ from the undisputed letters; many others hold that Paul wrote it, perhaps with Timothy’s help.
COL.date: If by Paul, about AD 54–63, from prison in Ephesus or Rome; if by a disciple, probably about AD 70–90.
COL.setting: Colossae was a small town in the Lycus valley of Phrygia (south-western Turkey), near Laodicea and Hierapolis (4:13). Its church had been founded by Epaphras, Paul’s co-worker (1:7). The false teaching it faced cannot be identified exactly; it seems to have mixed Jewish observances with speculation about angels and heavenly powers, and to have urged harsh self-denial. The letter is closely linked to Philemon, sharing many names, among them Onesimus (4:9), whose story Philemon tells.
themes: Christ, head of creation and of the Church
The fullness of God dwelling in Christ
Seeking the things that are above
Joy in suffering for the Church

key.note: The hymn to Christ, image of the invisible God
Paul’s sufferings fill up what is wanting of Christ’s, for the Church
In Christ dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily
Risen with Christ, seek the things that are above

sources: Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to Colossians

1TH.about: Probably the earliest of Paul’s letters and the oldest writing in the New Testament. Paul writes with warmth to a young church he had been forced to leave in haste, thanking God for their faith, charity and hope (1:3) and urging them to a holy and chaste life. He answers their grief over members who had died: the dead in Christ will rise, and we shall be always with the Lord (4:12–17). It closes with simple rules for Christian life: rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all things. The Church draws on it for her faith in the resurrection at Christ’s coming.
1TH.author: Paul, writing with Silvanus (Silas) and Timothy, who had shared in founding the church (1:1). Tradition and scholars agree: almost no one doubts that the letter is Paul’s own.
1TH.date: About AD 50–51, written from Corinth soon after Timothy came back from Thessalonica with good news (3:6; Acts 18:5).
1TH.setting: Thessalonica was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia, a busy port on the main Roman road across the Balkans. Paul preached there on his second missionary journey, but opposition soon drove him out (Acts 17:1–10). Most of the new Christians were Gentiles who had “turned to God from idols” (1:9), and they were now suffering at the hands of their neighbours. From Athens Paul sent Timothy to strengthen them; this letter is his grateful, relieved reply to the good news Timothy brought back.
themes: Hope for those who have died

key.note: Turned from idols to serve the living God and await his Son
This is the will of God, your sanctification
The dead in Christ will rise; we shall be always with the Lord
Always rejoice, pray without ceasing, in all things give thanks

sources: Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to 1 Thessalonians

2TH.about: A short second letter to the church at Thessalonica. Some there had been alarmed by claims, perhaps even by a letter falsely passed off as Paul’s, that the day of the Lord had already come (2:2). The letter steadies them: first must come a great revolt and “the man of sin” (2:3), held back for now by a restraining power the readers knew of; even St Augustine admitted he did not know what it was. Meanwhile they are to keep working and to hold fast the traditions they were taught, “whether by word or by our epistle” (2:14), a verse the Church cites in teaching on Tradition.
2TH.author: The letter names Paul, Silvanus and Timothy (1:1), and tradition has always received it as Paul’s. Scholars are divided. Many accept it as his, written soon after the first letter. Others think a disciple wrote it in his name some decades later, pointing to its close borrowing from 1 Thessalonians alongside a cooler tone and a different way of speaking about the end.
2TH.date: If by Paul, about AD 51, a few months after 1 Thessalonians; if by a later disciple, probably towards the end of the first century.
2TH.setting: The young church was still enduring persecution and trials (1:4). Talk of the Lord’s coming had unsettled it: some said the day had already arrived, and some had stopped working altogether, perhaps thinking the end was near, and were “curiously meddling” instead (3:11). The letter meets both problems. The end will not come without signs, and meanwhile Christians must work quietly, eat their own bread and not grow weary in doing good, keeping apart from those who walk disorderly.
themes: Signs before the day of the Lord
The dignity and duty of work

key.note: First a revolt and the man of sin, who shows himself as God
Hold the traditions taught by word or by letter
If any man will not work, neither let him eat

sources: Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to 2 Thessalonians

1TI.about: A letter of pastoral guidance from Paul to Timothy, his trusted helper, whom he had left in charge at Ephesus. It tells him how to silence false teaching, how the Church should pray (for all people, since God “will have all men to be saved”, 2:4), what kind of men may serve as bishops and deacons, and how to care for widows, slaves and the rich. With 2 Timothy and Titus it is called a Pastoral Letter. The Church has long drawn on it for the shape of the ordained ministry, and treasures its words on the Church as “the pillar and ground of the truth” (3:15).
1TI.author: The letter names Paul (1:1), and tradition received it as his, written between a first and a second imprisonment in Rome. Most scholars today think the three Pastoral Letters come from a follower of Paul after his death, since their vocabulary, style and church order differ from his other letters and they are hard to fit into the story told in Acts. Others defend Paul’s authorship, perhaps through a secretary.
1TI.date: If by Paul, about AD 63–66, between his two Roman imprisonments; scholars who see a later author usually date it about AD 80–100, some later still.
1TI.setting: Ephesus, a great port and the leading city of the province of Asia, had been a centre of Paul’s mission (Acts 19). Now some were teaching “fables and endless genealogies” (1:4), forbidding marriage and certain foods (4:3), and boasting of a “knowledge falsely so called” (6:20). The churches were becoming settled communities that needed tested leaders, ordered worship and care for the needy. Timothy, son of a Jewish mother and a Gentile father (Acts 16:1), is remembered by tradition as the first bishop of Ephesus.
themes: The Church, household of the living God
Godliness rather than love of money

key.note: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners
Pray for all; God wills all saved; one mediator, Christ Jesus
The Church, pillar and ground of truth; the mystery of godliness
Keep what is entrusted to you; avoid profane novelties

sources: Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to 1 Timothy

2TI.about: Paul’s farewell. Writing in chains and expecting soon to die (4:6), he urges Timothy, his “dearly beloved son”, to stir up the grace given him by the laying on of hands (1:6), to guard the faith entrusted to him, to bear hardship as a good soldier of Christ, and to preach the word in season and out of season. It holds the classic statement that all Scripture is inspired by God and profitable for teaching (3:16), and it ends with Paul’s own testimony: “I have fought a good fight: I have finished my course: I have kept the faith” (4:7).
2TI.author: The letter names Paul (1:1), and tradition holds that he wrote it during his last imprisonment in Rome, shortly before his martyrdom. Most scholars group it with the other Pastoral Letters as the work of a later follower. Some think it the likeliest of the three to be Paul’s own, or at least to preserve his personal messages in the final chapter.
2TI.date: If by Paul, about AD 64–67, shortly before his death under Nero; otherwise probably about AD 80–100, with the other Pastoral Letters.
2TI.setting: Paul is a prisoner in Rome (1:16–17), deserted by many, with only Luke beside him (4:11). He asks Timothy to come before winter and to bring the cloak he left at Troas, and his books (4:13). The Gospel’s preachers are suffering, and some in the Church are turning to teachers who tell them what their “itching ears” want to hear (4:3). Paul hands on his charge to the next generation of pastors, as a father to a son.
themes: Preaching the word in every season

key.note: Stir up the grace given by the imposition of my hands
Remember Christ risen: if we die with him, we shall live
All Scripture, inspired of God, is profitable to teach
I have fought a good fight; the crown of justice awaits

sources: Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to 2 Timothy

TIT.about: A short letter from Paul to Titus, whom he had left in Crete to set the young churches in order and to “ordain priests in every city” (1:5); the Greek has presbyters, that is, elders. It describes the kind of men these leaders must be, how Christians of every age and state should live, and why: because “the grace of God our Saviour hath appeared to all men” (2:11). Two of its passages, 2:11–14 and 3:4–7, are read at the Masses of Christmas night and dawn, celebrating God’s kindness shown in Christ and the new birth of baptism.
TIT.author: The letter names Paul (1:1), and tradition received it as his, written during travels after his first Roman imprisonment. As with 1 and 2 Timothy, most scholars today think a follower of Paul wrote it after his death; others defend Paul’s authorship. Titus was a Gentile convert (Galatians 2:3) and one of Paul’s most trusted helpers; tradition makes him the first bishop of Crete.
TIT.date: If by Paul, about AD 63–66; otherwise probably about AD 80–100, with the other Pastoral Letters.
TIT.setting: Crete, a large island south of Greece, had Christian communities whose beginnings are unknown; Cretans were in the crowd at Pentecost (Acts 2:11), and Acts shows Paul there only as a prisoner sailing for Rome. The letter warns of “vain talkers and seducers”, especially some of the circumcision party, teaching for gain (1:10–11), and quotes a Cretan prophet’s harsh verdict on his own people (1:12). Titus must appoint sound leaders and teach a way of life that wins outsiders’ respect for the Gospel.
themes: Grace that teaches us to live well
Baptism, the washing of new birth
Good works as witness to outsiders

key.note: Titus to ordain priests in every city; what a bishop must be
The grace of God has appeared, teaching us to live godly lives
Saved by God’s mercy through the laver of regeneration

sources: Lectionary for Mass, the Nativity of the Lord
Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to Titus

PHM.about: Paul’s shortest letter, and his most personal. Writing from prison, he sends back to his friend Philemon a slave, Onesimus, who had left his master and had since become a Christian through Paul (verse 10). Paul could command, but he appeals “for charity sake” (verse 9), asking Philemon to receive Onesimus “not now as a servant” but as “a most dear brother” (verse 16), and offering to repay any debt himself. Paul does not attack slavery as an institution, but the brotherhood he asks for undermines it from within.
PHM.author: Paul, writing with Timothy (verse 1). Virtually all scholars accept the letter as Paul’s own.
PHM.date: About AD 61–63 if written from Rome, as tradition holds; perhaps about AD 54–55 if, as some scholars think, from an imprisonment at Ephesus.
PHM.setting: Philemon was a Christian of some means, probably at Colossae in Asia Minor, whose house served as the meeting place of a church (verse 2). Slavery was woven into the Roman world, and a slave who left his master risked severe punishment. Paul, now “an old man” and a prisoner (verse 9), plays on the name Onesimus, which means “useful” (verse 11). Colossians 4:9 calls Onesimus “one of you” and sends him to Colossae with Tychicus.
themes: Brotherhood in Christ beyond social rank
An appeal of love, not command

key.note: Paul pleads for Onesimus, his son begotten in prison
No longer a slave, but a most dear brother
If he owes you anything, put it to my account

sources: Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to Philemon

HEB.about: A sermon in writing, which calls itself a “word of consolation” (13:22). It shows that Jesus, the Son through whom God has spoken his last word (1:1–2), is greater than the angels, than Moses and than the priests of the old covenant. He is the eternal high priest “according to the order of Melchisedech” (5:6), who offered himself once for all and entered heaven by his own blood. Chapter 11 praises the heroes of faith. The Church draws on Hebrews above all for her faith in Christ’s priesthood and in his one sacrifice, made present in the Mass.
HEB.author: The letter names no author. In Alexandria it was early counted among Paul’s letters, though its polished style differs from his; Origen judged the thoughts Paul’s but said only God knew who wrote it. The Latin West doubted it longer before receiving it as Paul’s, and it long stood as his fourteenth letter. Almost all scholars today, Catholics included, think another early teacher, perhaps of Paul’s circle, wrote it.
HEB.date: Probably before AD 96, the traditional date of Clement of Rome’s letter, which draws on it. Many date it before 70, since it speaks of the old sacrifices as still offered; others prefer the 80s.
HEB.language: Greek, the most polished in the New Testament
HEB.setting: Its first readers were probably Jewish Christians, as the ancient title says, though it would suit any believers steeped in the Old Testament. They had once borne insults and the loss of their goods with joy (10:32–34), but now some were growing weary and forsaking the assembly (10:25). The writer warns them not to drift back or fall away, for they have something better than the old worship. The greeting from “the brethren from Italy” (13:24) suggests a link with Rome.
themes: The one sacrifice of the new covenant
God’s last word in his Son

key.note: God, who spoke by the prophets, has now spoken by his Son
A high priest tempted in all things like us, yet without sin
Christ entered the Holies once, by his own blood
Faith, the substance of things to be hoped for

HEB.canon: Accepted early in the Greek East but long doubted in the Latin West, it was received everywhere by about AD 400. The Council of Trent lists it among the fourteen letters of Paul.
sources: Eusebius, Church History 6.14 and 6.25 (Clement of Alexandria, Origen)
Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to Hebrews

JAS.about: A practical letter, close in spirit to the wisdom books of the Old Testament and to the Sermon on the Mount. James asks for a faith that shows itself in deeds: be doers of the word and not hearers only (1:22), visit orphans and widows (1:27), never favour the rich over the poor, bridle the tongue. Its teaching that “faith without works is dead” (2:26) is read by the Church as completing Paul, not contradicting him, and the Council of Trent drew on it. The Church sees in 5:14–15 the apostolic witness to the Anointing of the Sick.
JAS.author: The writer calls himself “James, the servant of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1:1). Tradition identifies him with James, “the brother of the Lord” (that is, a kinsman), leader of the Jerusalem church, martyred about AD 62; Western tradition also counts him as the apostle James son of Alphaeus. Some scholars agree; many think a later Christian wrote in his name, noting its fine Greek and slow acceptance.
JAS.date: If by James, before AD 62, perhaps in the 40s or 50s, which would make it among the earliest New Testament writings; otherwise probably AD 70–100.
JAS.setting: It is addressed to “the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad” (1:1), most likely Jewish Christians living outside the Holy Land, though the phrase may stand for the whole Church as the new Israel. Its world is one of synagogue-like assemblies (2:2), quarrels and boasting, labourers cheated of their wages and rich men living in luxury (5:1–6). It names Jesus Christ only twice (1:1, 2:1), yet echoes his sayings throughout.

key.note: Be doers of the word and not hearers only
Pure religion: care for orphans and widows, unspotted from the world
Faith without works is dead
The priests of the Church pray over the sick, anointing them with oil

JAS.canon: Eusebius counts it among the books disputed in some churches; it was received in the canon lists of the late fourth century and confirmed by the Council of Trent.
sources: Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 10; Session 14, on Extreme Unction
Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to James

1PE.about: A letter of hope for Christians who suffer for their faith. Born again “unto a lively hope” by Christ’s resurrection (1:3), they are God’s own people, “a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood” (2:9), strangers and pilgrims in a world that misunderstands them. They are to do good, give a gentle answer for the hope within them, and rejoice to share Christ’s sufferings. Rich in baptismal language, the letter is a source of the Church’s teaching on the common priesthood of all the baptised and on Christ’s descent among the dead (3:19).
1PE.author: The letter names “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1), writing from “Babylon”, which ancient tradition and most scholars take as a name for Rome, with Silvanus and Mark at his side (5:12–13). It was accepted as Peter’s from the second century. Many scholars think his followers wrote it in Rome after his death, noting its polished Greek; others hold that Peter wrote it with Silvanus’s help.
1PE.date: If by Peter, in the early to mid 60s AD, before his martyrdom under Nero; if by his followers, probably about AD 70–90.
1PE.setting: It is addressed (1:1) to “strangers dispersed” through five regions of Asia Minor, today’s Turkey. Most were converts from paganism (1:18, 4:3), now slandered by neighbours who thought it strange that they no longer shared their revels (4:4). Their trial seems to have been local hostility more than an organised persecution, but to suffer “as a Christian” (4:16) was a real reproach. The letter teaches them to read their trials in the light of Christ’s Passion and to win others by their goodness.
themes: The royal priesthood of God’s people

key.note: Redeemed not with gold but with the precious blood of Christ
A chosen generation, a kingly priesthood, a holy nation
Always ready to give a reason for the hope within you
The devil, like a roaring lion, seeks whom he may devour

sources: Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to 1 Peter

2PE.about: A farewell letter in Peter’s name, written to strengthen believers against false teachers. It recalls the Transfiguration, which the apostles saw with their own eyes (1:16–18), and insists that prophecy came not by human will but from the Holy Spirit (1:21). To those who mocked the delay of Christ’s return it answers that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and that he waits out of patience, wishing all to repent (3:8–9). It speaks of God’s promise that we may become “partakers of the divine nature” (1:4), words much loved by the Fathers.
2PE.author: The letter names “Simon Peter” (1:1), recalls the Transfiguration, and calls itself his second letter (3:1); tradition received it as his. Even in the early Church some doubted it because its style differs from 1 Peter, as Jerome notes. Most scholars today think a disciple wrote it in Peter’s name after his death, as his testament; some still defend Peter’s authorship, perhaps through a different secretary.
2PE.date: If by Peter, shortly before his death in the mid 60s AD. Most scholars place it late in the first century or early in the second, perhaps making it the last New Testament book written.
2PE.setting: It speaks to Christians troubled by teachers who “deny the Lord” (2:1), turn freedom into licence and scoff: “Where is his promise or his coming?” (3:4). The first generation had died, and the world seemed unchanged. Chapter 2 shares much with the letter of Jude, which it probably draws on. Against such teaching the writer appeals to the apostles’ witness, to the prophets, and to Paul’s letters, in which some things are “hard to be understood” (3:16).
themes: Scripture inspired by the Holy Spirit
God’s patience and the Lord’s coming

key.note: Promises by which we are made partakers of the divine nature
Eyewitnesses of Christ’s glory on the holy mount
No prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation
One day as a thousand years; God wills all to repent

2PE.canon: One of the most doubted books in the early Church (Origen and Eusebius record the doubts), it was received in the canon lists of the late fourth century and confirmed by the Council of Trent.
sources: Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to 2 Peter

1JN.about: Less a letter than a sermon, written to strengthen a community shaken by division. It opens with testimony to “the word of life” that was seen, heard and touched (1:1), and returns again and again to two marks of true faith: believing that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, and loving one another. Only here does Scripture say “God is charity” (4:8, 4:16), the words with which Benedict XVI opened his first encyclical. It also teaches us to confess our sins, trusting in Christ, “an advocate with the Father” (2:1).
1JN.author: The letter names no author. From the second century (Irenaeus) tradition has ascribed it to John the Apostle, author of the fourth Gospel, whose language and thought it closely shares. Many scholars think it was written, some time after the Gospel, by a disciple formed in the Beloved Disciple’s circle; others keep the traditional attribution.
1JN.date: Probably about AD 90–110, after the Gospel of John; those who hold to John’s authorship place it in his old age at Ephesus, late in the first century.
1JN.setting: A group had broken away from the community: “They went out from us but they were not of us” (2:19). They seem to have denied that Jesus Christ had truly come in the flesh (4:2–3), and perhaps to have made light of sin and of the commandments. Tradition places the letter at Ephesus, where John lived in old age. The writer reassures those who stayed that they have the truth, the anointing of the Spirit and eternal life (5:13).
themes: God is light, God is love
Christ truly come in the flesh
Love of God shown in love of neighbour

key.note: What we have seen and touched of the word of life
If we confess our sins, he is faithful to forgive
Children of God now; we shall see him as he is
God is charity: he first loved us and sent his Son

1JN.canon: The words in 5:7 about three witnesses in heaven (the “Johannine Comma”), found in the later Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims, are absent from all early Greek manuscripts and the oldest Vulgate copies. Most scholars, Catholics included, think they began as a Latin gloss; the Church’s Nova Vulgata omits them.
sources: Raymond Brown, The Epistles of John (Anchor Bible)
Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to 1 John

2JN.about: With 3 John, one of the two shortest books of the Bible. “The Ancient”, that is, the Elder, writes to “the lady Elect and her children”, most likely a local church and its members, as the greeting from the children of “thy sister Elect” in the last verse suggests. He rejoices that some are walking in the truth, repeats the commandment heard from the beginning, that we love one another, and warns against deceivers who deny “that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh” (verse 7). Such teachers are not to be welcomed. Truth and love belong together.
2JN.author: The writer calls himself “the Ancient”, that is, the Elder or presbyter. Tradition identifies him with John the Apostle, author of 1 John, whose language and concerns this letter shares. Jerome reports that some early writers ascribed it to another John, known as John the Presbyter. Many scholars today see the Elder as a leader of the Johannine circle rather than the Apostle himself.
2JN.date: Probably about AD 90–110, close in time to 1 John.
2JN.setting: Early Christians met in houses and depended on travelling preachers. After a split in the Johannine communities (see 1 John 2:19), teachers who denied Christ’s true humanity were going from church to church. To receive such a teacher into the house where the church met, or to greet him with “God speed”, would be to share in his work (verses 10–11). The Elder hopes to visit soon and speak “face to face” rather than “by paper and ink” (verse 12).
themes: Christ truly come in the flesh

key.note: The Ancient greets the lady Elect, in truth and charity
The commandment from the beginning: love one another
Deceivers deny Christ come in the flesh; abide in his doctrine

2JN.canon: Eusebius lists it, with 3 John, among the books disputed in some churches, unsure whether it was by the evangelist or another John. Both were received in the canon lists of the late fourth century.
sources: Raymond Brown, The Epistles of John (Anchor Bible)
The Navarre Bible, introduction to 2 and 3 John

3JN.about: A private note from “the Ancient” to his friend Gaius, and with 2 John one of the two shortest books of the Bible. The Elder praises Gaius for walking in the truth and for welcoming travelling missionaries, who went out “for his name” taking nothing from the pagans (verse 7). He rebukes Diotrephes, a local leader who “loveth to have the preeminence” and refuses the Elder’s envoys, and commends Demetrius. It is the only New Testament book that does not name Jesus, yet it gives a rare glimpse of an early church’s hospitality, quarrels and love of the truth.
3JN.author: The same “Ancient”, or Elder, who wrote 2 John. Tradition identifies him with John the Apostle; Jerome reports that some early writers thought him another John, the Presbyter, and many scholars today see him as a leader of the Johannine circle rather than the Apostle himself.
3JN.date: Probably about AD 90–110, close in time to 2 John.
3JN.setting: Travelling preachers depended on local Christians for food and lodging as they carried the Gospel from town to town. In one church Diotrephes had refused to receive them, ignored a letter from the Elder, and put out of the church those who welcomed them (verses 9–10). Whether this was a quarrel over doctrine or over authority is unclear. Gaius, perhaps a member of a neighbouring church, is asked to keep sending such brothers on their way “in a manner worthy of God” (verse 6).
themes: Service rather than love of preeminence

key.note: No greater grace than to hear my children walk in truth
Receiving missionaries makes us fellow helpers of the truth
Diotrephes, who loves preeminence, refuses the brethren
Follow not evil but good: he that doth good is of God

3JN.canon: Eusebius lists it, with 2 John, among the books disputed in some churches; both were received in the canon lists of the late fourth century.
sources: Raymond Brown, The Epistles of John (Anchor Bible)
The Navarre Bible, introduction to 2 and 3 John

JUD.about: A short, urgent letter calling Christians “to contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints” (verse 3). Intruders were turning God’s grace into an excuse for immorality. Jude recalls examples of judgement from Scripture and Jewish tradition, from the fallen angels and Sodom to Cain, Balaam and Korah, and even quotes a prophecy from the Jewish Book of Enoch (verses 14–15). It ends with one of the most beautiful doxologies in the New Testament, giving glory to the God “who is able to preserve you without sin” (verses 24–25).
JUD.author: The writer calls himself “Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James” (verse 1). This points to Jude, one of the Lord’s “brethren”, or kinsmen, named in Mark 6:3, whom Catholic tradition has often identified with the apostle Jude Thaddeus. Some scholars accept his authorship; many think a later writer used his name, noting that verse 17 seems to look back on the apostles from a distance.
JUD.date: Uncertain. If by Jude, perhaps AD 50–70; many scholars prefer AD 80–100. It is probably earlier than 2 Peter, which seems to draw on it.
JUD.setting: The letter seems written for Christians at home in Jewish tradition. It draws freely on the Old Testament and on writings popular in its day, such as 1 Enoch and a story of Michael disputing with the devil over Moses’ body (verse 9). Men who had “secretly entered in” (verse 4) were sharing in the community’s meals (verse 12), living immorally and despising authority. Jude urges the faithful to build on their holy faith, pray in the Holy Spirit and keep themselves in God’s love (verses 20–21).
themes: Grace is not a licence to sin

key.note: Contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints
Enoch’s prophecy: the Lord comes with thousands of his saints
Build on your faith, pray in the Holy Ghost, keep in God’s love
Praise of God, who can preserve you without sin

JUD.canon: Some in the early Church doubted it because it quotes the Book of Enoch, as Jerome notes, and Eusebius counts it among the disputed books; it was received in the canon lists of the late fourth century. Its quotation does not make Enoch part of the Catholic canon.
sources: Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to Jude

REV.about: The last book of the Bible, a prophecy in the language of visions and symbols. It is not a coded timetable of the end of the world. It unveils, for churches under pressure, the hidden meaning of history: Christ, the Lamb who was slain and lives (5:6), already reigns, and evil, however strong, will fall. Its scenes of heaven’s worship, the woman clothed with the sun, the fall of Babylon and the new Jerusalem end in the cry “Come, Lord Jesus” (22:20). The Church sees her liturgy joined to the worship of heaven it describes.
REV.author: The seer calls himself John, exiled on the island of Patmos (1:9). From the second century (Justin, Irenaeus) tradition has identified him with John the Apostle. In the third century Dionysius of Alexandria argued from its very different Greek that another John wrote it. Most scholars today see him as a Christian prophet named John, perhaps linked with the Johannine circle; some still hold that he was the Apostle.
REV.date: Most likely about AD 95, late in the reign of Domitian, as Irenaeus reports; some scholars prefer the late 60s, soon after Nero’s persecution.
REV.language: Greek, unusual in style and strongly coloured by Hebrew
REV.setting: It is addressed to seven churches in the Roman province of Asia, in today’s western Turkey (chapters 2–3). Their members were under pressure to honour the emperor as a god and to share in pagan feasts; some compromised, some were poor and harassed, and one faithful witness, Antipas, had been killed (2:13). In the manner of Jewish apocalyptic writing, rich in images from Daniel, Ezekiel and Exodus, John shows that Rome’s power, which most interpreters see behind the beast and Babylon, will pass, while the faithful reign with Christ.
themes: Christ the Lamb, slain and victorious
Heaven’s worship and the Church’s liturgy
The new heaven and new earth

key.note: The Lamb standing as if slain, worshipped by all heaven
A woman clothed with the sun, seen as Mary and as the Church
A new heaven and a new earth: God dwells with his people
Surely I come quickly. Amen. Come, Lord Jesus

REV.canon: Called the Apocalypse in the Douay-Rheims, from its Greek title meaning “unveiling”. Received early in the West, it was doubted for a time in parts of the Greek East, but it is included in the canon lists of Athanasius (367) and of the Councils of Hippo and Carthage.
sources: Lectionary for Mass, the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary
Raymond Brown, An Introduction to the New Testament
The Navarre Bible, introduction to Revelation
